name: Neuroendocrine liver metastases
lead: Which pathway this patient belongs to once differentiation and grade are known, and what the liver is allowed to be asked to do over a disease measured in years.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 1 · Differentiation and grade
crit: Biopsy reporting differentiation, an exact Ki-67 index and a mitotic count
Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT for receptor status and whole-body staging
Functional syndrome recorded explicitly, confirmed with directed tests
Hepatic burden and distribution: unilobar versus bilobar, resectable versus diffuse-miliary
Primary site, whether it is resected, and the extrahepatic sites
gates.ask: Is this a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour or a poorly differentiated carcinoma, and do I have the Ki-67 to prove it?

standard.t: Get a biopsy with the Ki-67 index and the mitotic count, read by a pathologist experienced in neuroendocrine neoplasms, and have differentiation stated explicitly rather than inferred from grade.
standard.pref: Every patient before a pathway is assigned, and again on any specimen sampled metachronously — a well-differentiated G3 tumour and a poorly differentiated carcinoma can share a Ki-67 range and need different pathways.
standard.avoid: Do not accept a report giving Ki-67 as a range, and do not let grade stand in for differentiation; if the report does not say which it is, ask the pathologist before the board meets.
standard.note: Downgraded to C on the full-text read. The requirement is right but its evidence is consensus, not comparison: NANETS 2017 means a show of hands from a 15-member panel with no evidence grading and no systematic literature search, and consensus was recorded only that both differentiation and grade be reported, with a significant majority — 75% or more — that both mitotic rate and Ki-67 be measured and fine-needle aspiration accepted as adequate in most cases. The Ki-67 55% figure that ENETS 2023 calls the best discriminator between carcinoma and well-differentiated G3 is drawn from a single report, and the same paper concedes morphology can be ambiguous, particularly for large-cell carcinoma. A mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm is named as such, and its clinically dominant aggressive component sets the pathway.

standard.t: Stage with somatostatin-receptor PET/CT, 68Ga-DOTATATE or equivalent, alongside cross-sectional CT or MRI.
standard.pref: All patients at staging and at restaging: it is the gateway to both the analogue and the PRRT decisions, and the EANM consensus judged it necessary at staging of all NET as complementary to conventional imaging.
standard.avoid: Do not use receptor uptake as a substitute for anatomic burden assessment or as a universal response measure, and do not order octreotide SPECT/CT unless SSTR-PET is unavailable.
standard.note: Graded B on diagnostic accuracy rather than on outcome: NANETS 2017 reports 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT sensitivity of 95% against 31% for octreotide SPECT, which is why the substitution is made. The EANM position itself is a modified three-round Delphi vote — necessary at staging of all NET in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%), CT or MRI also necessary in 20 of 23 (87.0%) — with consensus set at 70% agreement for a single answer and only 50% preference in multiple-choice format, and consensus failed on 12 of 43 questions. The panel was drawn from high-volume centres with full access to Ga-68 tracer and PRRT, so availability is assumed rather than tested. Where SSTR-PET has not been done, the board records its absence explicitly rather than proceeding as if it had.

standard.t: Record carcinoid syndrome, insulinoma, gastrinoma or any other functional syndrome explicitly, confirmed with tests directed at the suspected syndrome rather than a panel of every available marker.
standard.pref: Before any hepatic procedure — this changes procedural safety planning, not only symptom management, and high hepatic burden with a midgut primary is the dominant carcinoid-crisis risk combination.
standard.avoid: Do not treat a normal marker panel as excluding a functional syndrome, and do not leave the syndrome undocumented because symptoms are currently controlled on an analogue.
standard.note: Grade D: a named local requirement with no comparative outcome evidence behind the thresholds themselves.

standard.t: State the hepatic tumour burden, unilobar versus bilobar, resectable versus diffuse-miliary pattern, the primary site and whether it is resected, the extrahepatic sites, and which problem is driving the clinical picture.
standard.pref: Every case at submission: burden and distribution decide whether cytoreduction, embolotherapy or transplantation is even on the table.
standard.avoid: Do not open a treatment discussion where the dominant problem has not been named — hormonal symptoms and tumour progression need different answers and conflating them produces treatment without an endpoint.

alt.t: Obtain FDG PET where the grade is high, where behaviour is discordant with grade, where SSTR uptake is heterogeneous, or where a CT or MRI lesion shows no SSTR uptake.
alt.pref: Before committing to receptor-directed therapy in G2–G3 disease or rapid progression, to find receptor-negative, FDG-avid disease that PRRT will not treat.
alt.avoid: Not for routine staging of well-differentiated disease, where NANETS found no value in it.
alt.note: The roadmap keeps FDG selective on the Itanet triggers rather than requiring it for every G2–G3 PRRT candidate as EANM Focus 3 does. EANM endorsed FDG before PRRT in G2–G3 to exclude mismatched FDG-positive, SSTR-negative lesions in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%) by modified Delphi, and Itanet grades the FDG trigger 3b-A. What neither establishes is that acting on the mismatch changes outcome: EANM's extension of PRRT into G3 rests on two small retrospective series confined to Ki-67 under 55%, and EANM reached no consensus at all on PRRT with mismatched lesions.

alt.t: Consider re-biopsy on unexpected behavioural change or discordant FDG avidity.
alt.pref: Where the original grading is years old or the disease has clearly changed pace: grade progression and transformation both occur and change the pathway.
alt.avoid: Not as a scheduled ritual — no study defines the trigger or the interval, which is why this sits at C and remains an open local decision.
alt.note: Itanet attaches 3a-A to re-evaluation before radioligand therapy when behaviour changes, which is stronger than the roadmap's 'consider'; whether it becomes a required step before PRRT is a ratification item.

avoid.t: Do not assign a pathway on grade alone.
avoid.pref: The differentiation fork drives every later decision, so the tissue standard is deliberately set high.
avoid.avoid: If differentiation cannot be established on the available material, get more material rather than guessing from Ki-67.

avoid.t: Do not manage a poorly differentiated carcinoma on the indolent-disease pathway.
avoid.pref: Carcinoma is managed as an aggressive carcinoma. In the SEER figures ENETS 2023 reproduces, median survival is 33.9 months for stage I–II, 16.3 months for stage III and 5.2 months for distant disease, with 5-year survival 42%, 25.6% and 4.7%; metastatic patients survive a median 11 to 12 months on palliative platinum–etoposide and about 1 month without it. Performance status then dominates: median survival 18 months at PS 0, 12 at PS 1 and 5 at PS 2.
avoid.avoid: Somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative intent, PRRT, hepatic debulking for cytoreduction and transplantation are all inappropriate here. Managing a carcinoma on the indolent pathway costs months of ineffective therapy in a disease measured in months. Note what the recommendation is made of: ENETS grades both the advice against metastasectomy and the advice against PRRT in metastatic digestive NEC 5D, its weakest grade, resting on no comparative data, and well-differentiated G3 NET is outside that paper's scope by design — so the guidance is strongest exactly where the diagnosis is unambiguous and silent where it is not.

gates.name: 2 · G1–G2, low burden: treat or observe
crit: Well-differentiated NET, grade 1 or grade 2
Low hepatic tumour burden, resectable or ablatable
Radiologically stable or slowly progressive
Asymptomatic, or symptoms attributable to a hormonal syndrome rather than to bulk
gates.ask: This patient has three small liver lesions and no symptoms — do I start an analogue, operate, or scan again in three months?

standard.t: Start a somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative effect and symptom control.
standard.pref: Receptor-positive or functional phenotypes, and anyone in whom progression would be hard to salvage. PROMID (n=85, treatment-naive midgut) gave time to progression 14.3 versus 6.0 months, hazard ratio 0.34 (95% CI 0.20–0.59); CLARINET (n=204, non-functioning enteropancreatic, Ki-67 under 10%) gave a progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.47 (0.30–0.73) with 24-month progression-free survival 65.1% versus 33.0%.
standard.avoid: Do not make it mandatory for every patient. Grade A applies to the antiproliferative indication in unresectable disease: PROMID and CLARINET enrolled only patients with no curative option, unresectable disease or declined surgery. In resectable or ablatable disease, analogue versus resection or ablation is an MDT decision.
standard.note: Neither trial established an overall-survival benefit — CLARINET found no significant difference in overall survival or quality of life, and PROMID is an interim analysis at 67 progressions and 16 deaths of a trial that enrolled 85 of a planned 162 patients and was then closed for slow accrual, so its confirmatory survival analysis at 121 deaths was never performed. The effect is stabilisation, not shrinkage: one partial remission per arm in PROMID, and objective remissions with an analogue are rare. For a liver pathway the decisive limitation is that PROMID's effect was concentrated where there was least liver to treat — hazard ratio 0.17 (0.08–0.40) at 0 to 10% hepatic involvement, 0.40 (0.10–1.67) at 10 to 50% and 0.71 (0.11–4.45) above 50%, with 95% of patients having Ki-67 of 2% or less and 61% having 10% or less liver involvement. CLARINET held across hepatic volume, hazard ratio 0.45 (0.22–0.91) above 25%, but that dichotomy is a post hoc simplification of a prespecified five-category variable whose component hazard ratios ran 0.24 to 0.54. For carcinoid-syndrome control the source is ENETS 2024, not these trials.

opts.name: Observation with scheduled imaging
opts.when: NCCN says observation with serial imaging is an option if the patient has a low tumour burden; ENETS 2024 supports watch and wait only for selected G1, asymptomatic, low-burden and/or stable small-intestine NET at B-2b, ESMO restricts it to Ki-67 under 2% with low burden and stable disease [IV, A], and ASCO puts the evidence strongest at Ki-67 under 10% with imaging every 3 to 6 months. The three thresholds do not agree with one another and none was derived.
opts.pref: Asymptomatic, low-volume, radiologically stable disease: cross-sectional imaging every 3 to 4 months at first and about every 6 months once stability is shown, with treatment started on progression or symptoms. The CLARINET placebo arm itself ran a median 18.0 months without progression.
opts.avoid: Not where the syndrome is active, where receptor-positive bulk is accumulating, or where the patient will not reliably return for imaging. The 3–4-month interval is a local choice within the NCCN range of every 12 weeks to 12 months.
opts.note: The NANETS midgut panel split roughly half and half between starting an analogue and observing, and concluded that either is acceptable — that is a recorded absence of consensus, not a positive endorsement. The strongest quantitative support for observing is the CLARINET placebo arm itself, which ran a median 18.0 months without progression and which ASCO notes can be read as support for watch and wait in favourable-biology patients; against that, only 22% of one watch-and-wait cohort ENETS cites ever needed surgery.

opts.name: Hepatic cytoreduction — resection, ablation, or both
opts.when: Reasonable consideration, grade C: aim for maximal debulking with parenchymal-sparing resection and resect the primary where appropriate. The supporting series are single-arm with strong selection.
opts.pref: Burden that can largely be cleared in a patient fit for a long operation, where the target and the expected residual can be named before the incision — see gate 5 for the thresholds and what supports them.
opts.avoid: Poorly differentiated carcinoma, diffuse miliary disease, uncontrolled extrahepatic progression, significant untreated carcinoid heart disease. Do not offer it as an alternative to an analogue on the strength of the debulking survival figures.
opts.note: The expanded-criteria series reported 5-year disease-specific survival 90% and median liver progression-free survival 71.6 months in 52 selected patients; these are the outcomes of selected patients, not a measured treatment effect, and within that series the extent of debulking did not correlate with liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37). ENETS 2024 puts the same recommendation at B-4 — a surgical approach in stage IV G1/G2 liver-only disease if R0 is achievable — on 5-year overall survival of 71 to 74%, and 85% for R0 resections, while recording recurrence after R0 of about 80% at 5 years. ESMO attributes that 85% partly to preselection bias and notes liver metastases are often more extensive than appreciated even intraoperatively.

alt.order: Observation is listed first because the guidelines treat it as an equally acceptable course in this phenotype, not because it outperforms anything; cytoreduction is second because its evidence is single-arm. Neither order reflects a survival advantage — no randomised comparison of debulking against systemic therapy alone exists.
alt.flagnote: Whether observation with 3–4-monthly imaging is an acceptable documented alternative to an immediate analogue, and whether grade B is the right label for it, is alignment area 3 and remains a ratification item.

avoid.t: Do not read debulking series survival figures as a treatment effect.
avoid.pref: Present them to patients as the outcomes of selected patients: single-arm, heavily selected, with no randomised comparison against systemic therapy alone.
avoid.avoid: Quoting 90% 5-year disease-specific survival as what an operation delivers.

avoid.t: Do not offer Y90 radioembolisation without a phenotype-specific rationale.
avoid.pref: Selected early use may be appropriate where the rationale is stated — lobar or segmental liver-dominant distribution, or prior Whipple or biliary instrumentation.
avoid.avoid: Low-burden disease in a patient with years of treatment horizon ahead: radiation-induced liver injury accrues over exactly the time the patient has. Imaging signs of cirrhosis-like morphology or portal hypertension appeared in 15 of 52 patients (29%) followed beyond a year, more often after bilobar treatment, though no single imaging finding reached significance and the series was not powered for it. Read the denominator: of 93 patients treated, 41 had under a year of follow-up, so the long-term toxicity estimate is survivor-biased, and no radioembolisation-induced liver failure occurred in that series or in the 148-patient multicentre series.

gates.name: 3 · G1–G2, high burden or progressing
crit: Diffuse or bilobar hepatic disease
Progression on a somatostatin analogue
Clinically significant hepatic burden driving the picture
Hormonal symptoms poorly controlled on an analogue
gates.ask: Which problem am I treating here — the tumour burden or the hormone — and what is this liver procedure meant to achieve?

standard.t: Continue the somatostatin analogue for functional-syndrome control where it is needed, and after clinically significant progression in a nonfunctional tumour do not automatically continue it for antiproliferative benefit.
standard.pref: Functional disease, where the analogue is doing hormonal work that nothing else in the plan replaces.
standard.avoid: Carrying an analogue indefinitely in a nonfunctional tumour that has progressed on it, on the assumption that it is still holding the tumour back.
standard.note: Downgraded to C: this is a position taken in the absence of evidence rather than from it. The NANETS midgut panel reached no consensus on continuing an analogue past progression, and no trial has tested continuation after documented progression in either direction — PROMID and CLARINET both enrolled patients who were not progressing, 96% of CLARINET patients having had no progression in the 3 to 6 months before randomisation. The roadmap's position is that the indication after progression is hormonal, not antiproliferative; that is a defensible reading of what the trials enrolled, not a demonstrated equivalence.

standard.t: Escalate systemically on progression, with the agent chosen by primary site, receptor status, growth rate and burden — see gate 6.
standard.pref: Receptor-positive midgut disease progressing on an analogue: 177Lu-DOTATATE. Pancreatic primaries: sunitinib or capecitabine–temozolomide. Everolimus across non-functional GI and lung disease.
standard.avoid: Do not treat the grade as a survival claim for any one agent: NETTER-1's final overall-survival analysis gave median 48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.17), p=0.30, and did not meet its endpoint. Every other agent in the sequence is a progression-free survival result too, and ASCO rated overall-survival certainty very low for CLARINET, RADIANT-3, RADIANT-4 and the sunitinib trial and low for NETTER-1.
standard.note: Downgraded from A to B. The class of systemic escalation is expected practice, but every ASCO recommendation covering it is graded weak on low or moderate evidence quality, and ASCO states outright that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any sequence after progression. §6 sets out what each trial actually showed.

alt.t: Add a liver-directed procedure where the hepatic goal is stated: bland embolisation or conventional TACE for symptoms, progression or bulky liver-dominant disease, Y90 for selected lobar or segmental distribution.
alt.pref: Liver-dominant bulk or a hormonal syndrome poorly controlled on an analogue, where the viable target, the goal, the liver-function cost, the owner and the reassessment date can all be named — see gate 7 for the modality choice. The largest technique comparison is retrospective and non-randomised: in 69 carcinoid patients bland embolisation gave a radiologic response of 81.0% against 44.4% for chemoembolisation (multivariate odds ratio 6.41, 95% CI 1.97–20.84, P=0.002) with no difference in progression-free or overall survival, while in 54 islet-cell patients chemoembolisation trended better on response and survival without reaching significance and those patients had more resected primaries and less liver involvement.
alt.avoid: Do not group bland embolisation, conventional TACE and radioembolisation as equivalent, and do not use drug-eluting embolics in NET.
alt.note: NCCN NE-H accepts bland embolisation and conventional TACE and advises against drug-eluting embolics because of increased hepatobiliary toxicity in the NET population. Comparative superiority of bland versus conventional chemoembolisation remains unresolved, and the two ENETS papers on the page point in opposite directions: the 2024 small-intestine guidance generally prefers bland embolisation, while the 2023 functioning-pancreatic guidance says chemoembolisation is possibly more effective. Treatment choice in the supporting series was made by the referring physician, so the apparent technique effects are confounded with who was sent where.

avoid.t: Do not add a liver-directed procedure on systemic progression without a stated hepatic goal.
avoid.pref: The trigger for a liver-directed procedure is a hepatic problem — bulk, symptoms, a dominant growing lesion — not the fact that a drug has failed.
avoid.avoid: A repeat embolic or radiation cycle with no named target, goal, liver-function cost, owner or reassessment date. Worsening liver function after embolic or radiation therapy is a stop, not a reason to change device: cumulative hepatic injury is the limiting resource in a long-horizon disease.

gates.name: 4 · High-grade disease: G3 NET or carcinoma
crit: Ki-67 above 20%
Poorly differentiated small-cell or large-cell morphology
Grade progression from a prior G1 or G2 tumour
A mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm
gates.ask: Ki-67 is 34% — is this a well-differentiated G3 tumour I can treat with receptor-directed therapy, or a carcinoma that needs platinum tomorrow?

opts.name: 177Lu-DOTATATE, well-differentiated G3, receptor-positive
opts.when: Preferred for a defined phenotype, and note which one: NETTER-2 (n=226) enrolled newly diagnosed, inoperable, SSTR-positive, well-differentiated GEP-NET with Ki-67 10–55% diagnosed within the previous 6 months, no patient having progressed on a prior analogue, and gave median progression-free survival 22.8 versus 8.5 months by blinded central review, stratified hazard ratio 0.276 (0.182–0.418), p<0.0001, with objective response 43.0% versus 9.3% and 8 complete responses (5%) versus none.
opts.pref: Receptor uptake greater than normal liver in the target disease, Ki-67 inside 10–55%, renal, marrow and hepatic reserve documented, and clinically significant burden — the last being a local selection criterion, not a trial entry criterion.
opts.avoid: Ki-67 above 55% was not studied. Receptor-negative or FDG-avid, SSTR-negative disease will not be treated by it: NETTER-2 required uptake score 3 or 4 in all target lesions, so heterogeneous-uptake disease was never enrolled. It also excluded any previous hepatic artery embolisation or radiofrequency ablation, which excludes a large part of the population this page's gate 7 creates. In a series of 69 receptor-expressing high-grade neoplasms, median progression-free survival was 9.6 months and overall survival 19.9 months, falling to 4 and 7 months once Ki-67 exceeded 55%.
opts.note: Graded B, not A: NETTER-2 is open-label with a median follow-up of 23.2 months, overall survival not reached in either group with 48% of control patients crossed over, no difference in time to deterioration of global health status, diarrhoea, fatigue or pain, and a comparator of high-dose octreotide 60 mg that the authors themselves describe as giving only 4 to 8 months of progression-free survival in grade 3 NET. There is no comparison with the alkylating chemotherapy a board would weigh first line in a high-grade pancreatic NET, and 123 of 226 patients (54%) had pancreatic primaries. NETTER-1's final overall-survival analysis was negative (48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84, p=0.30). NETTER-2 enrolled 147 grade 2 patients with Ki-67 10–20% and 79 grade 3 patients at a median Ki-67 of 16%, so the same evidence covers G2 tumours in that band. Itanet grades the same NETTER-2 recommendation 1b-A and EANM supported first-line PRRT only in a minority of highly selected patients (17 of 22, 77.3%); the roadmap's downgrade to B is a ratification item.

opts.name: Capecitabine–temozolomide, or platinum-based therapy
opts.when: Reasonable alternative where behaviour is aggressive and receptor expression is low or absent. E2211 (n=133, pancreatic, progression within 12 months) met its primary endpoint at an interim analysis with an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119 in a phase 2 trial designed at a two-sided significance level of 0.20: median progression-free survival 22.7 versus 14.4 months with temozolomide alone, hazard ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.36–0.93), P=.022. The final analysis at a median 59.9 months gave 23.2 versus 15.1 months, hazard ratio 0.71 (0.46–1.07).
opts.pref: High burden, tumour-related symptoms or rapid progression, especially with a pancreatic primary; and where receptor imaging will not support PRRT.
opts.avoid: Do not apply a universal platinum regimen to all G3 NET — Itanet reports etoposide–platinum efficacy as limited in advanced G3 NET compared with its use in carcinoma, and ASCO records that platinum–etoposide has little supporting evidence in well-differentiated G3 disease. In E2211 overall survival was not significant (53.8 versus 58.7 months, hazard ratio 0.82, P=.42; a significant interim difference, hazard ratio 0.41, P=.012, did not persist), the response rate did not differ from temozolomide alone (39.7% versus 33.8%, P=0.59) and grade 3–4 treatment-related toxicity doubled, 45% versus 22%.

standard.order: PRRT is listed first for the receptor-positive Ki-67 10–55% phenotype because that is the phenotype a randomised trial tested; chemotherapy is first where receptor expression is low or growth is fast. The order reflects the trials' entry criteria and a progression-free survival result, not a demonstrated survival advantage for either.
standard.flagnote: The roadmap does not state whether hepatic debulking is appropriate in well-differentiated G3 disease, which is the decision a liver surgeon will face. Both NANETS surgical papers advise against cytoreducing G3 liver metastases — NANETS 2017 refers grade 3 liver metastases for systemic therapy, and NANETS 2020 says poorly differentiated carcinoma should not be resected while localised well-differentiated G3 tumours may be resected within multimodal therapy, with liver cytoreduction often not indicated because of high relapse and poor survival. NANETS 2020 states in the same breath that its well-differentiated G3 recommendations are unsupported, pending studies using the 2017 WHO classification, and that grade 2 disease is not a contraindication. Alignment area 15 asks whether G3 debulking should be added to the Avoid column except for selected limited disease within multimodal therapy.

standard.t: Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma: platinum–etoposide systemic therapy, managed as an aggressive carcinoma.
standard.pref: Small-cell or large-cell carcinoma morphology, whatever the hepatic burden. Carboplatin–etoposide first line gives response 30 to 50%, progression-free survival 4 to 6 months and overall survival 11 to 12 months.
standard.avoid: Somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative intent, PRRT, hepatic debulking for cytoreduction and transplantation are all inappropriate. ENETS grades the recommendation against metastasectomy and against PRRT in metastatic digestive NEC 5D — its weakest grade, resting on no comparative data — but it is the statement that would close down a liver resection discussion at board. Almost every therapeutic recommendation in that paper is 4B or weaker and no randomised trial underpins either first- or second-line therapy.
standard.note: Molecular profiling of advanced high-grade disease, where available, may identify additional treatment options. A prior history of G1 or G2 NET strongly favours G3 NET over carcinoma if G3 disease is confirmed.

alt.t: In carcinoma, use liver-directed therapy only for a specific symptomatic or oligoprogressive problem, with a stated goal and a stated duration.
alt.pref: A single bleeding, painful or obstructing deposit in a patient whose systemic disease is otherwise being controlled.
alt.avoid: Cytoreduction for its own sake, or any liver-directed plan without an end date, in a disease whose median survival on treatment is about a year.

avoid.t: Do not assume an overall-survival benefit from the PRRT trials.
avoid.pref: State plainly what they showed: NETTER-1 met progression-free survival decisively — hazard ratio 0.18 (0.11–0.29) on health-authority re-review of baseline scans, updated from the published 0.21 (0.13–0.33) — and did not meet overall survival (48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.60–1.17, p=0.30); NETTER-2 met progression-free survival with a large effect and its overall survival is immature, with 48% of control patients crossing over.
avoid.avoid: Telling a patient that PRRT has been shown to make them live longer. In NETTER-1 the proportional-hazards assumption failed (Schoenfeld residuals p=0.03), 36% of controls crossed over and 32% received 177Lu-dotatate specifically, so the final comparison is closer to early versus delayed PRRT than to PRRT versus none; the crossover-adjusted hazard ratio was 0.73 (0.40–1.34). Overall survival was a secondary endpoint powered for 158 deaths and the 5-year calendar cutoff arrived first at 142, and the restricted-mean-survival analysis that carries the authors' positive message was added by protocol amendment and does not exclude zero at 5 years (5.1 months, 95% CI -0.5 to 10.7).

avoid.t: Do not apply a universal platinum regimen to all G3 NET, and keep surgery and transplant criteria distinct from systemic-treatment options.
avoid.pref: Phenotype-based G3 options: receptor status, growth rate and primary site choose the drug.
avoid.avoid: Treating well-differentiated G3 as carcinoma, or reading eligibility for a G3 systemic option as eligibility for cytoreduction or transplantation.

gates.name: 5 · Hepatic cytoreduction
crit: Well-differentiated NET, not poorly differentiated carcinoma
A substantial fraction of the hepatic burden can be cleared — the target and the expected residual named before operating
No diffuse-miliary pattern and no uncontrolled extrahepatic progression
Adequate performance status and hepatic reserve, with significant carcinoid heart disease addressed first
Demonstrated local experience with parenchymal-sparing hepatic surgery
gates.ask: Can I clear enough of this liver to be worth the operation, and what exactly am I leaving behind?

standard.t: Operate for meaningful reduction of hepatic burden with parenchymal-sparing resection — often multiple small wedges — using ablation as an adjunct for lesions unsuited to resection, and resect the primary where appropriate.
standard.pref: Well-differentiated disease where a substantial fraction of the burden can be cleared and the patient will tolerate a long operation. The expanded-criteria series of 52 patients reported 5-year disease-specific survival 90%, 5-year overall survival 88% and median liver progression-free survival 71.6 months (95% CI 56.0–87.3) with a 5-year liver progression-free rate of 64%, with 51 of 52 having wedge resections and 47 bilobar resections, median 15 tumours resected, median largest metastasis 2.5 cm and 65% having extrahepatic disease. ENETS 2024 makes the parallel recommendation for stage IV G1/G2 liver-only disease where R0 is achievable at B-4.
standard.avoid: Poorly differentiated carcinoma, diffuse miliary disease, uncontrolled extrahepatic progression, poor performance status, hepatic dysfunction, or liver replacement above roughly 50 to 70% — where NANETS says embolisation, PRRT or medical therapy are preferable. Debulking must not be called complete eradication.
standard.note: Read the series with its limits in front of you. It is retrospective, single-surgeon and single-institution; the debulking percentage is the operating surgeon's own intraoperative visual and ultrasonographic estimate, not a volumetric or blinded radiological measurement, and the same surgeon selected who was operated on at all. Decisively, patients in whom the surgeon judged intraoperatively that 70% was not achievable were not resected, so the series contains no sub-70% group and cannot test the threshold it is used to justify. Within it, extent of debulking did not correlate with liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37), progression rates were 27.3%, 27.3% and 31.6% across the 70–89%, 90–99% and 100% groups (P=.95), complete resection of all gross disease was achieved in only 12 of 52 (25%) and conferred no advantage, and the only variable that predicted anything was age — 5-year liver progression-free survival 25.7% under age 50 versus 85% at 50 or older (P=.001). The lowest-debulking group contains 11 patients, no morbidity or mortality rate is reported anywhere in the paper, only a median length of stay of 6 days, median follow-up was 37.4 months against a median liver progression-free survival of 71.6 months, and 88% were kept on octreotide LAR, which the authors themselves say may account for the unusually long progression-free survival rather than the debulking strategy. ENETS 2023 puts the target at 70 to 90% or more of visible disease with adequate liver function at level 2b, grade B, and gives no guidance on which end of that 20-point range applies to whom; ENETS 2024 does not address the 70 versus 90 question at all. Recurrence after an R0 resection in this disease runs about 80% at 5 years, so lifelong follow-up is part of the operation.

opts.name: Thermal ablation as complete local treatment
opts.when: Selected oligometastatic complete local treatment, usually four lesions or fewer each under 3 cm as NCCN describes it; ENETS 2024 puts percutaneous ablation at three to five metastases each under 3 cm at B-3. Neither limit comes from the series that support ablation: those enrolled up to 15 tumours, up to 10 cm, with under 20% liver volume involved, a mean largest tumour of 3.6 cm and a mean of six lesions treated. Cure evidence is weak.
opts.pref: Limited well-differentiated disease where all known sites can be addressed, alone or combined with resection, with safe access and margins — an upfront local option for suitable oligometastatic disease, or focal salvage, not necessarily after every systemic treatment. Quote local control per patient as well as per lesion: local recurrence at an ablated site occurred in 7 of 63 patients (11%) and in 22% of 89 patients, against per-lesion rates of 6.3% and 7.9%. Morbidity was 5% and 5.6% with one 30-day death (1%) in the larger series and a mean hospital stay of 1.1 days.
opts.avoid: Do not call it cure: 80% of the 45 patients with imaging follow-up in one series developed new or progressive liver disease, mostly growth of sub-centimetre lesions deliberately left untreated, and in the larger series 63% developed new liver lesions and 59% developed extrahepatic disease. Neither series reports grade or Ki-67 at all — at the published discussion the authors confirmed the analysis had not been done — and both pool medullary thyroid carcinoma (9 and 11 patients) and bronchial carcinoids with gastroenteropancreatic disease, so long survival after ablation reflects indolent biology and multimodality salvage as much as the procedure. Record residual disease and grade.
opts.note: More often the realistic goal is cytoreduction, symptom control or treatment of a growing dominant lesion; symptom relief was reported in 94% at one week with a median duration of 11 months in the smaller series, and in 97% with 73% significant or complete and a median 14 months in the larger. Survival in these series is not attributable to the ablation: during follow-up 30% had an analogue, 27% a repeat ablation, 18% chemotherapy and 10% chemoembolisation, and median follow-up of 30 months sits against a 6-year median survival.

opts.name: Resection of the primary tumour with liver metastases present
opts.when: NCCN says resection of ileum or jejunum NETs with their mesenteric nodes should be performed when symptoms arise from the primary, and should be considered in asymptomatic cases to reduce future obstruction, mesenteric ischaemia, bleeding or perforation.
opts.pref: Small-bowel primaries, where NANETS reached full consensus that resection should be considered when feasible on retrospective medians of 7.4 versus 4.0 years, 9.9 versus 4.7 years and 159 versus 47 months favouring resection; and before PRRT where mesenteric ischaemia or obstruction risk is real. Transplant candidacy depends on the primary being out.
opts.avoid: No universal resect-or-observe instruction for pancreatic primaries: NANETS 2020 reached no consensus, with the majority holding that resection may help only in selected circumstances — functional tumour, body or tail location, local complications. ENETS notes that at least three propensity-matched studies show no survival benefit in asymptomatic stage IV disease.
opts.note: The supporting series are retrospective with unresected patients older, more comorbid or more heavily replaced; NANETS states that selection bias cannot be excluded, and ENETS adds that only 22% of a watch-and-wait cohort ever needed surgery. The roadmap keeps selected primary surgery after MDT review and distinguishes small-bowel from pancreatic decisions.

alt.order: These are adjuncts to and alternatives within the same operation, not a ladder: ablation is listed with resection because the roadmap pairs them, and primary resection is a separate decision taken at the same board. Neither order carries a survival claim.
alt.flagnote: The hepatic burden threshold above which cytoreduction is not attempted is unresolved local decision 3. The two numbers in circulation have different parentage and neither is evidence-derived. The 90% figure, which NCCN still prints, came from an observation about symptom relief and was never validated as an oncologic threshold. The 70% figure was set by the NANETS 2017 panel on two retrospective single-institution series from the centres that championed it, with one dissenting vote, and the series most often cited for it excluded by design every patient in whom 70% was not achievable. NANETS 2020 reached no consensus on the threshold for pancreatic primaries at all, over half the panel favouring an individualised 70% and a minority questioning whether any benefit of cytoreduction has been established. Registry tracking: burden before and after, residual, liver progression-free survival.

avoid.t: Do not call debulking complete eradication, and do not operate without naming the target and the expected residual first.
avoid.pref: It is worth doing only if a substantial fraction of the burden can be cleared; say what fraction and what will be left before the patient consents.
avoid.avoid: An operation whose success is defined after the fact by what turned out to be resectable.

avoid.t: Do not debulk in poorly differentiated carcinoma, diffuse miliary disease, or uncontrolled extrahepatic progression.
avoid.pref: Systemic therapy is the pathway in carcinoma; in diffuse disease that cannot reach a meaningful clearance, embolisation, PRRT or medical therapy are preferable.
avoid.avoid: Significant carcinoid heart disease is a contraindication to hepatic cytoreduction until it is addressed — raised right-sided pressure increases the risk of liver surgery, and NCCN advises valve replacement before liver resection where carcinoid heart disease is significant. Do not extend the list beyond what the panels said: NANETS 2020 holds that extrahepatic disease by itself should not contraindicate resection of the primary or hepatic cytoreduction, because it is rarely the cause of death, and that grade 2 disease in the primary or the liver metastases is not a contraindication either.

gates.name: 6 · Systemic therapy: what each trial showed
crit: Progression on a somatostatin analogue
Unresectable disease with no liver-directed goal to serve
Receptor-positive disease being considered for PRRT
A pancreatic primary needing a sequencing decision
gates.ask: I have four drugs and no trial that compares them — what decides the order for this patient?

opts.name: 177Lu-DOTATATE
opts.when: NCCN: lutetium Lu 177 dotatate is FDA-approved for SSTR-positive GEP NETs including foregut, midgut and hindgut tumours. NETTER-1 (n=229, midgut jejunoileal or proximal colon disease, Ki-67 20% or less, progressing on standard-dose octreotide) met progression-free survival decisively — 65.2% versus 10.8% progression-free at month 20, hazard ratio 0.21 (0.13–0.33), updated to 0.18 (0.11–0.29) on health-authority re-review, median not reached versus 8.4 months, objective response 18% versus 3%.
opts.pref: Receptor-positive disease with uptake greater than normal liver in the target disease on SSTR PET, renal, marrow and hepatic reserve documented before each course, and surgical evaluation first — especially where mesenteric ischaemia or obstruction is a risk. NANETS and Itanet both prefer it second line in SSTR-positive midgut disease.
opts.avoid: The final overall-survival analysis did not meet its endpoint: 48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.17), p=0.30. The label is wider than the trial: only midgut primaries were enrolled, so the foregut and hindgut indications rest on retrospective and registry data, which is also why EANM declined to recommend PRRT second line for pancreatic NET and why ESMO places it in pancreatic NET only after failure of approved therapies [III, A]. Avoid generally at GFR under 30 and use with caution at GFR 30 to 50. Where SSTR uptake is heterogeneous, a CT or MRI lesion shows no uptake, or progression is rapid, get FDG PET first to find receptor-negative disease PRRT will not treat.
opts.note: EANM requires Krenning 3 or 4 uptake in all metastases; the comparator in NETTER-1 was octreotide LAR 60 mg, a dose never shown to control tumour growth, so the trial does not compare PRRT with everolimus, chemotherapy or liver-directed therapy. Eligibility was set by 111In-octreotide scintigraphy, not by the 68Ga- or 64Cu-DOTATATE PET used today. Myelodysplastic syndrome occurred in 2 of 111 treated patients, one fatal at 33 months and the only treatment-related death, with no control denominator because adverse-event reporting during long-term follow-up was required only in the PRRT arm; ASCO puts treatment-related myeloid neoplasia after PRRT at about 2.6% and ESMO reports up to 3 to 4% irreversible marrow toxicity and 30% long-term grade 1 or 2 renal toxicity. EANM reached no consensus on the right time point for PRRT in the sequence, and did not recommend it specifically second line for pancreatic NET.

opts.name: Everolimus
opts.when: RADIANT-3 (n=410, pancreatic): progression-free survival 11.0 versus 4.6 months, hazard ratio 0.35 (0.27–0.45). RADIANT-4 (n=302, non-functional GI and lung): 11.0 versus 3.9 months, hazard ratio 0.48 (0.35–0.67).
opts.pref: Non-functional disease across primary sites, and where receptor-negative biology or haematologic risk rules out PRRT.
opts.avoid: No survival benefit is established. RADIANT-3's overall survival is uninterpretable — 73% of the placebo arm crossed over — and RADIANT-4's interim overall survival was a first look at 70 deaths against a planned 191, hazard ratio 0.64 (0.40–1.05), one-sided p=0.037 against a boundary of 0.0002. RADIANT-4 excluded carcinoid syndrome and pancreatic primaries and 30% of patients had lung primaries with only 23% ileal and 8% jejunal, so it does not cover the functional small-bowel patient who most often reaches a liver surgeon. The cost is real: dose reduction or interruption in 67% versus 30%, non-infectious pneumonitis of any grade in 16%, and discontinuation for grade 3–4 drug-related events in 12% versus 3%.
opts.note: The benefit is stabilisation, not shrinkage: confirmed objective response 5% in RADIANT-3 and 2% in RADIANT-4. The size of the effect depends on who read the scans — in RADIANT-4 central review gave 11.0 versus 3.9 months and local review 14.0 versus 5.5 — and in RADIANT-3 progression-free survival data were censored in 47% of the everolimus arm against 19% of placebo with 2.3 times the exposure. Both trials excluded patients embolised within 6 months or ablated within 2 months, so neither says anything about combining everolimus with liver-directed therapy.

opts.name: Sunitinib, pancreatic primaries
opts.when: n=171, well-differentiated pancreatic NET with documented progression in the previous 12 months: progression-free survival 11.4 versus 5.5 months, hazard ratio 0.42 (0.26–0.66), P<0.001; overall survival hazard ratio 0.41 (0.19–0.89).
opts.pref: Progressive pancreatic NET where a tyrosine kinase inhibitor suits the comorbidity profile.
opts.avoid: Closed early by the data and safety monitoring committee at 171 of 340 planned patients and 81 of 260 planned events after more deaths and serious adverse events with placebo; the observed statistic did not cross the prespecified efficacy boundary (z 3.85 against 3.88), so the headline result never formally met the protocol threshold. Censoring was heavily imbalanced (65% versus 40%), response was investigator-assessed with no central review in a trial unblinded at closure, and 59 placebo patients crossed to open-label sunitinib, so the survival signal cannot be taken at face value. Ki-67 was evaluable in only about 42% of patients. A 9.3% response rate means it stabilises rather than shrinks — it will not convert unresectable hepatic disease.

opts.name: Capecitabine–temozolomide, pancreatic primaries
opts.when: E2211 (n=133): 22.7 versus 14.4 months against temozolomide alone, hazard ratio 0.58 (0.36–0.93), P=.022, declared at an interim analysis with an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119 in a phase 2 trial designed at a two-sided significance level of 0.20; final analysis 23.2 versus 15.1 months, hazard ratio 0.71 (0.46–1.07).
opts.pref: Pancreatic primaries with high burden, tumour-related symptoms or rapid progression, which is where ASCO places it first line; MGMT deficiency was associated with response, 52% versus 15%, though both arms contained temozolomide so it cannot be called predictive.
opts.avoid: Phase 2, open label, not powered for overall survival, which was not significant (53.8 versus 58.7 months, hazard ratio 0.82, P=.42) after a significant interim difference failed to persist; the response rate did not differ from temozolomide alone (39.7% versus 33.8%, P=0.59), so this is not the agent to choose when shrinkage is the object. Grade 3–4 toxicity doubled, 45% versus 22%, with seven second primary cancers including one myelodysplastic syndrome. The control arm was single-agent temozolomide, never a standard of care, so the trial does not compare the combination with everolimus, sunitinib or PRRT.

opts.name: Cabozantinib, after PRRT or targeted therapy
opts.when: CABINET, placebo-controlled 2:1: extrapancreatic cohort (n=203) 8.4 versus 3.9 months, hazard ratio 0.38 (0.25–0.59); pancreatic cohort (n=95) 13.8 versus 4.4 months, hazard ratio 0.23 (0.12–0.42).
opts.pref: Late line, after PRRT, everolimus or sunitinib: patients had a median of two to three prior lines and 59% had already had 177Lu-dotatate.
opts.avoid: Objective response was 5% and 19%, and there was no overall-survival benefit — 21.9 versus 19.7 months, hazard ratio 0.86 (0.56–1.31), and 40.0 versus 31.1 months, hazard ratio 0.95 (0.45–2.00) — with 33% and 41% of placebo patients crossing over. Grade 3 or higher adverse events ran 62 to 65% versus 23 to 27%, two-thirds needed dose reduction to a median of about 38 mg against the assigned 60 mg, and four patients in the extrapancreatic cabozantinib group had a grade 5 event judged at least possibly treatment-related. The trial stopped early at interim on local rather than central assessment — a different endpoint from the one reported as primary — with only 111 of 164 planned events in the extrapancreatic cohort, and 7 pancreatic patients were registered into the extrapancreatic cohort and 3 the other way.

standard.order: The order follows primary site and receptor status, not survival: receptor-positive disease first to PRRT, pancreatic primaries to sunitinib or capecitabine–temozolomide, non-functional disease to everolimus, cabozantinib after those. Every one of these is a progression-free survival result. There is no randomised evidence establishing a sequence and the roadmap does not claim one — sequencing is driven by primary site, receptor status, growth rate, hepatic burden, the need for rapid shrinkage, prior therapy, toxicity tolerance and access.
standard.flagnote: Whether first-line PRRT is offered for receptor-positive grade 2–3 disease, and to whom, is unresolved local decision 2: one open-label randomised trial with a progression-free survival endpoint, overall survival immature. Registry tracking: every PRRT course, progression-free survival, hepatic and renal function. Itanet grades PRRT over targeted agents 2b-B and over chemotherapy 3b-A on cross-trial comparison; ESMO records that one of its own authors dissented on PRRT sequencing.

standard.t: Document somatostatin-receptor uptake greater than normal liver in the target disease, and renal, marrow and hepatic reserve, before every PRRT course.
standard.pref: PRRT is receptor-dependent: uptake above normal liver is the NCCN threshold and EANM asks for Krenning 3 or 4 in all metastases.
standard.avoid: Do not spend marrow, renal and hepatic reserve on FDG-avid, receptor-negative disease that PRRT will not treat; assess discordant FDG-positive, SSTR-negative lesions first. Surgical evaluation should be performed before PRRT.
standard.note: Prior liver-directed therapy may raise PRRT hepatotoxicity, and the safe sequence of radioembolisation and PRRT is unresolved — NANETS states plainly that cumulative hepatic radiation from radioembolisation followed by PRRT is unstudied, so cumulative hepatic exposure is reviewed before either. NETTER-2 excluded any prior hepatic artery embolisation or ablation outright, so the first-line PRRT evidence does not describe a patient who has already had liver-directed therapy.

alt.t: Hepatic debulking before PRRT may improve response and progression-free survival, and reduces the mass of amine-producing cells before a radioligand course.
alt.pref: A fit patient with high hepatic burden and a functional syndrome facing PRRT, where cytoreduction is independently justified.
alt.avoid: Do not build a debulking indication on this alone: NANETS/SNMMI attributes it to limited retrospective data, and the crisis-prevention argument comes from a narrative review whose own institutional audit of 127 administrations recorded no carcinoid crisis at all.
alt.note: This is the one place where the surgeon sits inside the PRRT safety pathway rather than beside it.

avoid.t: Do not claim a sequence the evidence does not support.
avoid.pref: Record the order chosen and the reason for it at tumour board for each patient, and track it in the registry.
avoid.avoid: ASCO states explicitly that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any particular sequence after progression, because the trials used placebo controls with almost no head-to-head comparisons; overall-survival certainty was rated very low for CLARINET, RADIANT-3, RADIANT-4 and the sunitinib trial and low for NETTER-1, chiefly because of crossover, which ASCO puts at 85% in RADIANT-3 and 69% in the sunitinib trial. ESMO records that one of its own authors held PRRT should come earlier in SSTR-positive pancreatic NET.

avoid.t: Do not continue a somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative benefit in every nonfunctional NET after significant progression.
avoid.pref: Continue it for hormonal control where the tumour is functional.
avoid.avoid: PROMID and CLARINET tested delay of progression in stable, indolent disease — 96% of CLARINET patients had no progression in the 3 to 6 months before randomisation — and neither establishes an antiproliferative role after documented progression.

gates.name: 7 · Liver-directed therapy: which modality
crit: Bulky or symptomatic liver-dominant disease
Hepatic progression with a stated hepatic goal
Hormonal symptoms poorly controlled on a somatostatin analogue
Lobar or segmental distribution, or prior Whipple or biliary instrumentation
gates.ask: This liver needs treating — which device, and what does it cost me in reserve later?

opts.name: Bland embolisation or conventional TACE
opts.when: NCCN: there are no completed randomised studies comparing TAE with conventional TACE and both are acceptable. An accepted liver-control and hormone-symptom strategy in well-differentiated NET, for symptoms or progression on an analogue or other systemic therapy, and for bulky disease without waiting for progression.
opts.pref: Bulky or symptomatic liver-dominant disease — an early liver-directed choice, not universally second line to PRRT, Y90 or ablation. In a retrospective series of 123 patients treated between 1992 and 2000, radiologic response by WHO criteria was 66.7% in carcinoid versus 35.2% in islet-cell tumours (P<0.0001) with no complete response in any carcinoid patient, median progression-free survival 22.7 versus 16.1 months and median overall survival 33.8 versus 23.2 months. Within the carcinoid group bland embolisation outperformed chemoembolisation on response, 81.0% versus 44.4% (odds ratio 6.41, 1.97–20.84, P=0.002), with no difference in progression-free or overall survival. Plan staged treatment, liver reserve, biliary infection precautions and a carcinoid-crisis response.
opts.avoid: Serious adverse events followed 25 embolisation sessions (8.5%) in 19 patients in that series — hepatorenal syndrome in 7, sepsis in 6, hepatic abscess in 2 and one death — and major complications ran 27.3% where liver involvement exceeded 75% against 12.9% below it, a difference that did not reach significance (P=0.11). ENETS 2024 generally prefers bland embolisation in small-intestine NET; ENETS 2023 says the opposite for functioning pancreatic NET, calling chemoembolisation possibly more effective.
opts.note: Comparative superiority of bland versus conventional chemoembolisation remains unresolved; choose by burden, symptoms, reserve and biliary infection risk, and do not group the approaches as equivalent. Technique in the supporting series was chosen by the referring physician, not randomised, and in the islet-cell group the chemoembolisation patients had more resected primaries, less liver involvement and more sessions, so the apparent advantage may be selection. The series predates RECIST, analogue maintenance, PRRT and 68Ga-DOTATATE staging, and reports no grade or Ki-67 anywhere.

opts.name: Radioembolisation — Y-90 or holmium-166
opts.when: Revised local position, Reasonable consideration: selected lobar or segmental liver-dominant control, not restricted to last resort. A phenotype-selected alternative to bland or conventional chemoembolisation, which may be used earlier when justified; NCCN permits it especially for lobar or segmental distribution or prior Whipple or biliary instrumentation, where embolic infection risk may be lower.
opts.pref: Lobar or segmental liver-dominant disease with a positive rationale stated. In a 10-centre series of 148 patients and 185 treatments, imaging response at 3 months was partial in 112 treatments (60.5%) and complete in 5 (2.7%), with median survival 70 months from first treatment. Adding 166Ho-SIRT to PRRT in 24 matched pairs gave 2-year hepatic progression-free survival 82% (57–96) versus 50% (28–72) and best objective response 71% versus 25%.
opts.avoid: Weigh late hepatic injury, bilobar treatment, prior radiation and future PRRT. Imaging signs of cirrhosis-like morphology or portal hypertension appeared in 15 of 52 patients (29%) followed beyond a year, more often after bilobar treatment though no single finding reached significance, and ALP and AST elevations were still present in the 11 followed beyond four years. In that same single-centre cohort of 93 patients median survival was 28.0 months, not 70, and baseline findings changed the conversation entirely: 7.3 months with ascites versus 53.8 without, and 21.1 months with extrahepatic disease versus 58.0 without. A long expected survival raises the threshold for radioembolisation rather than lowering it.
opts.note: The 70-month median cannot be read as a treatment effect — 78% of patients were alive at a median follow-up of 42 months, response assessment was not standardised and used CT, MRI or scintigraphy with each investigator giving a best estimate where WHO or RECIST could not be applied, participation was voluntary and half the patients came from self-described centres of excellence. Neither Y90 series reports grade or Ki-67. The HEPAR PLuS comparison was a prospective single-arm cohort against a retrospective control with only 24 of a planned 120 pairs matched, median liver tumour burden 8% versus 20% so the population was not uniformly bulky, no overall-survival benefit and medians unseparated, a higher proportion of deaths in the combination arm, toxicity analyses abandoned for reporting bias, every combination patient dropping at least one ECOG point after PRRT before SIRT, and funding from Terumo with two co-authors employed by Terumo. There is no evidence for or against the safety of sequencing radioembolisation and PRRT.

opts.name: Thermal ablation
opts.when: Selected oligometastatic complete local treatment, usually four lesions or fewer each under 3 cm; otherwise cytoreduction, symptom control or treatment of a growing dominant lesion.
opts.pref: Safe access, achievable margins, all sites reviewed and a hormone-syndrome plan in place — an upfront local option for suitable oligometastatic disease, or focal salvage.
opts.avoid: Separate complete treatment from debulking: there is no established cured fraction, local recurrence per patient was 11% and 22% against per-lesion rates of 6.3% and 7.9%, and long survival after ablation is strongly affected by indolent biology, multimodality salvage and entry criteria that selected the least burdened patients — under 20% liver volume, at most 15 tumours, at most 10 cm.

standard.order: Do not use a universal ablation, SBRT, Y90, TACE, HAI, histotripsy ladder. An upfront alternative chosen because of anatomy or organ reserve is not a post-progression second line. The order here reflects how often each is reached for in liver-dominant NET and the wording of NCCN NE-H, not any survival advantage — no optimal order has been established for combining PRRT, systemic therapy and liver-directed treatment, and a liver-directed procedure does not replace indicated systemic therapy. After progression or toxicity, restage and reconsider complete treatment rather than automatically repeating the same procedure.
standard.flagnote: Two ratification items sit here. Which embolisation technique is the programme's default is unresolved decision 1: one small randomised TAE versus TACE trial (Maire 2012, 26 patients, cited from ENETS rather than read in full) found no significant 2-year progression-free survival difference but was underpowered, the only prospective three-way comparison is still running, and any choice is expertise and availability. Whether the programme offers radioembolisation at all, and at what point, is unresolved decision 4 — a mandatory exhaustion-of-all-options rule before Y90 is a local restriction and not NCCN. Note also that the shared liver-directed matrix carries RETNET outcome figures: the RETNET paper in this depot is the study protocol and reports no outcome data of any kind, so no efficacy figure on this page is attributed to it, and the matrix entry should be corrected at its source.

alt.t: SBRT or ablative radiotherapy can provide local treatment of selected liver targets in well-differentiated NET, particularly where access or anatomy prevents ablation.
alt.pref: An alternative focal therapy, or control of oligoprogression, with the continuing systemic or PRRT strategy coordinated.
alt.avoid: Evidence is mainly retrospective and there is no established tumour-specific curative benefit. An exceptional plan to treat all oligometastatic disease is labelled definitive local intent with uncertain cure, not proven curative treatment.
alt.note: There is no NET-specific series; the matrix entry for this modality rests on mixed-histology data.

avoid.pref: Bland embolisation or conventional TACE instead, chosen by burden, symptoms, reserve and biliary infection risk.
avoid.avoid: NCCN says drug-eluting embolics are associated with increased hepatobiliary toxicity in the NET population and are not recommended. The phase 2 DEB-TACE study stopped on its safety endpoint: 7 of 13 patients (54%) developed a biloma, 6 of them after the first procedure, four needed percutaneous drainage, and two had a prolonged infected hospital course and subsequently died.
avoid.note: Downgraded to C because of what the ban is made of. The 13-patient trial is a single-centre interrupted interim analysis with no usable confidence interval around either the 54% biloma rate or the 78% per-lesion response rate; bilomas occurred in the patients with roughly one third the hepatic tumour burden of those without (mean 12% versus 44%, P=0.06), beads were mixed 1:1 with contrast and were invisible on injection with the endpoint judged by operator tactile feedback, and the authors concede this may have caused overembolisation and non-target deposition. The 54% figure is far out of line with the comparator literature the paper itself cites — about 30% biliary injury with none needing drainage in one drug-eluting series and 0% in another using 500 to 700 micrometre particles — so the signal may be technique and bead size rather than the device class. The position is kept because the harm is biliary and irreversible and two patients died; it is a precautionary institutional choice, not a demonstrated class effect. RETNET in the depot is the study protocol and reports no outcome data at all. Its drug-eluting-bead arm was later closed for increased severe complications — reported in the ENETS 2024 guidance, not in the protocol paper — so the trial's practice-changing message came from its 20% serious-adverse-event stopping rule rather than its efficacy question.

avoid.t: Hepatic arterial infusion has no routine role in this indication.
avoid.pref: Consider only within a disease-specific study or as an exceptional expert indication.
avoid.avoid: Do not transfer colorectal or intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma pump evidence across histologies; there is no dedicated NELM data.

avoid.t: Histotripsy is investigational here: trial or institutional registry only.
avoid.pref: Only with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, device-compliant target size and depth, an independent standard-treatment review, and functional-syndrome precautions.
avoid.avoid: FDA device clearance for tumour destruction does not establish survival benefit or equivalence to established ablation, and there is no tumour-specific curative evidence. A bridge-to-transplant use remains protocol-based: a technical response does not establish transplant eligibility.
avoid.note: The HOPE4LIVER one-year update reported local control of 63.4% on the primary assessment against 90% post hoc in 47 patients with 52 tumours of mixed histology.

gates.name: 8 · Functional syndrome and crisis precautions
crit: Carcinoid syndrome or any other documented functional syndrome
Markedly raised 5-HIAA or chromogranin A
Any planned hepatic procedure, ablation or PRRT course in functional disease
Signs or symptoms of carcinoid heart disease
gates.ask: Who owns the crisis plan for this operation, and is the rescue drug actually in the room?

standard.t: Write a procedure-specific crisis plan with a named owner, available rescue octreotide and immediate haemodynamic treatment, for every functional tumour.
standard.pref: Every procedure in a functional patient — surgery, ablation, embolisation and PRRT, with anaesthesia and nuclear medicine determining the precautions for each. Treatment is intravenous octreotide 500 to 1000 micrograms at symptom onset, repeated every 5 minutes until control and escalated to a continuous infusion if refractory.
standard.avoid: Do not let a plan live in individual memory; this is a named safety process that fails exactly when it is informal. It is not an evidence question and carries no comparative outcome evidence — audit it for adherence.
standard.note: Highest risk: midgut primary, high hepatic tumour burden, liver metastases, raised 5-HIAA or chromogranin A, prior carcinoid syndrome including carcinoid heart disease, advanced age, and concurrent histamine-releasing drugs. Crisis usually appears 12 to 48 hours after a first PRRT dose but has followed later doses. The source is a narrative review — no search dates, strings, study selection or quality appraisal are reported — whose management advice rests on case reports and small series, with no consensus recorded on how many boluses precede an infusion, on steroid prophylaxis, or on whether PRRT should be re-attempted after a crisis.

standard.t: Give short-acting octreotide before embolisation in patients with hormonal syndromes.
standard.pref: Functional disease going to bland embolisation, conventional TACE or radioembolisation: short-acting octreotide 250 to 500 micrograms subcutaneously, or 50 micrograms intravenously, 1 to 2 hours before the procedure.
standard.avoid: Octreotide within 48 hours, or octreotide LAR within 28 days, of 177Lu-dotatate can competitively block tumour uptake and reduce efficacy, and no rule defines when prophylaxis is worth that trade-off — decide it explicitly with nuclear medicine rather than by default.
standard.note: NCCN preserves pre-embolisation octreotide for hormonal syndromes; the roadmap keeps it while refusing the wider claim that prophylaxis prevents crisis.

standard.t: Assess the syndrome and the heart before hepatic procedures, with joint cardiology and anaesthesia review where carcinoid heart disease is significant.
standard.pref: Annual echocardiography once serotonin or 5-HIAA exceeds about five times the upper limit of normal, and a low threshold in anyone with signs or symptoms. NCCN: in significant carcinoid heart disease, valve replacement should be done before liver resection if at all possible.
standard.avoid: Do not take a functional patient to hepatic resection or transplant evaluation with right-heart disease unassessed — NANETS treats significant carcinoid heart disease as a contraindication to hepatic cytoreduction, because raised right-sided pressure increases the risk of liver surgery.
standard.note: This closes a gap the earlier draft acknowledged. Whether an explicit echocardiography gate is adopted is alignment area 12 and remains a ratification item.

alt.t: Debulking by surgery, interventional radiology or external-beam radiotherapy before a radioligand course is a recognised preventive measure, alongside correction of electrolyte, nutritional and protein deficits.
alt.pref: High hepatic burden with a midgut primary and an active syndrome, where cytoreduction is justified on its own terms.
alt.avoid: Not as a reason to operate on a patient who would not otherwise be a cytoreduction candidate: the evidence is a narrative review and a single retrospective series.

alt.t: For refractory carcinoid diarrhoea with stable imaging, telotristat ethyl rather than raising the analogue dose.
alt.pref: Diarrhoea that persists on a standard-dose analogue while imaging is stable — the hormone problem, not the tumour problem. NANETS reached consensus on this from TELESTAR, in which telotristat ethyl 500 mg three times daily reduced daily bowel movements by 35%.
alt.avoid: Escalating the analogue dose for diarrhoea and calling it tumour control; state which problem is being treated.

avoid.t: Do not rely on prophylactic octreotide to prevent intraoperative carcinoid crisis, and never let it delay fluids and vasopressors.
avoid.pref: Be ready to manage crisis with fluids and vasopressors — vasopressin, phenylephrine — as well as octreotide, and treat preparedness rather than prophylaxis as the safeguard.
avoid.avoid: NCCN states prophylactic octreotide is likely ineffective in preventing intraoperative carcinoid crisis, NANETS 2017 says prevention has not been established, and NANETS 2020 calls the role of analogues in preventing crisis in pancreatic NET undefined.
avoid.note: The roadmap's quoted 1 to 2% incidence during 177Lu-dotatate comes from a narrative review whose authors state the diagnosis lacks agreed criteria and whose own 127 administrations over five years produced no crisis at all — its single adverse event was bronchospasm in a patient with endobronchial carcinoid, attributed to crisis or not on clinical reasoning alone. Surgical series cited by NANETS report intraoperative event rates of 24 to 30% despite octreotide, with liver metastases the strongest predictor in one of them. The NANETS 2017 octreotide recommendation is internally conflicted, stating that the literature does not support prophylaxis while sanctioning an intraoperative infusion of 100 to 500 micrograms per hour as harmless practice. Whether §7 is reframed as crisis preparedness for every patient with neuroendocrine liver metastases is alignment area 11.

gates.name: 9 · Transplant candidate
crit: Well or moderately differentiated G1/G2 NET, Ki-67 under 20% and mitotic rate under 20 per 10 high-power fields
Gastroenteropancreatic primary with portal venous drainage, resected together with all extrahepatic disease, no recurrence for at least six months

gates.ask: Is this patient inside the transplant criteria, and is it our protocol or the allocation route that stops us?

standard.t: Offer transplantation only within a trial or prospective registry, under restrictive criteria, through the nonstandard Adult Transplant Oncology Review Board route scored at MMaT-3.
standard.pref: A young patient with liver-limited, unresectable, well-differentiated disease whose primary has been out for at least six months without recurrence, who has shown stability under observation, and who will be entered in the registry. In the Milan series 280 referrals produced 88 patients meeting Milan-NET criteria, of whom 42 were transplanted and 46 were not, the split driven by waiting-list capacity, age and patient refusal: 5- and 10-year overall survival were 97.2% and 88.8% with transplantation versus 50.9% and 22.4% without, median not reached versus 62 months. A later single-centre comparison from the same unit, 104 Milan-in patients of whom 48 were transplanted and 56 resected, found 10-year survival 93% versus 75% and disease-free survival 52% versus 18%.
standard.avoid: Allocation eligibility does not establish routine clinical benefit, and NCCN deems liver transplantation investigational, acknowledging the considerable associated risks. Neuroendocrine liver metastasis is not a standardised OPTN MELD exception: use the nonstandard 'other liver cancer or tumour, specify' pathway with a written narrative, and confirm the current OPTN policy text before any listing decision.
standard.note: Read the evidence with its selection in view. Allocation in the Milan series was non-randomised, recipients were 15 years younger (median 40.5 versus 55.5 years) in a cohort where age was itself an independent predictor of death, and 18 of the 22 patients who declined transplant did so because they judged their own health normal, so the comparison arm is self-selected on wellbeing. Propensity score could not be matched on in 88 patients and entered only as a covariate; the adjusted transplant survival benefit was 6.82 months at 5 years (95% CI 1.10–12.54) rising to 38.43 months at 10 years (21.41–55.45), with an adjusted hazard ratio for death without transplant of 7.4 (2.4–23.0). The non-transplant arm predates current therapy — 8.7% had PRRT, 2.2% targeted agents, none had cytoreductive liver resection — and WHO 2010 review reclassified 8.7% of them as G3 against 0% of recipients. 37 of 42 grafts (88%) were marginal quality. The resection comparison reports univariate analysis only, with transplant recipients younger, more heavily involved (59% versus 21% above 25% liver involvement), higher Ki-67, node-positive primaries in 79% versus 18%, and selected by a test of time — median 38.5 months from primary resection to liver surgery versus 6.5 months — while the resection arm had no routine lymphadenectomy and 11% R1. Six of the nine deaths after transplantation were attributed to transplant sequelae rather than cancer. Sufficient to justify a protocol; not sufficient to make transplantation a routine option.

standard.t: Hold the allocation record and the renewal ownership from the start: diagnosis and histology, baseline burden, primary and last-treatment dates, serial response imaging, extrahepatic staging, request and extension dates, score route, and named coordinator and physician sign-off.
standard.pref: Every candidate from first submission. MMaT means median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run, not a fixed national score; an MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15 under Policy 9.4.E, and exceptions generally require 90-day extensions under 9.4.C.
standard.avoid: Do not let the imaging-timing wording drift. The guidance requires radiologic workup for extrahepatic disease 'at least 3 months prior to initial or extension MELD exception request (submit date)', including somatostatin-receptor scintigraphy or Ga-68 imaging or PET; that wording is reproduced rather than changed to 'within three months', and the intended timing is confirmed with the review process before filing while current clinical staging is kept.
standard.note: Reassess eligibility at progression, recurrence, new extrahepatic findings and each extension. Exploratory laparoscopy or laparotomy is not required for the exception.

alt.t: Where disease is limited enough to clear, compare resection and cytoreduction against transplantation at the same board before listing.
alt.pref: Favourable-biology patients are often cytoreduction candidates too, and organ scarcity limits transplantation; ENETS 2024 reduces transplantation to a rare consideration in selected individuals after resecting the primary to leave liver-only disease.
alt.avoid: Do not list a patient whose disease a hepatectomy would clear — limited disease amenable to curative liver resection excluded 75 of 280 referrals in the Milan series.
alt.note: Recurrence after transplantation is predominantly extrahepatic and late (median disease-free interval 78 months, with the liver involved in 2 of 25 recurrences) while after resection it is intrahepatic and early (24 months, liver involved in 37 of 42); 17 of 19 resection deaths were cancer-related, almost all from intrahepatic progression to liver failure. That contrast is the strongest argument for transplantation on this page, and it comes from an unadjusted comparison of two cohorts accrued over 36 years.

avoid.t: Do not list G3 disease or neuroendocrine carcinoma, any extrahepatic disease, a patient whose primary is still in place, a patient with no documented observation period, or a patient not entered in the registry.
avoid.pref: Local policy, stated as policy rather than as evidence. Extrahepatic progression, including new Ga-68-positive lymph nodes, calls for delisting; reconsideration may be possible after all extrahepatic disease is resected and absent for at least six months, while extrahepatic solid-organ metastases such as lung or bone are described as permanent exclusion.
avoid.avoid: Do not treat a local complete response after liver-directed therapy as an automatic transplant exception, and record bridge or downstaging separately from definitive local treatment.
avoid.note: Any centre age or hepatic tumour-burden cutoff must be labelled local or attributed to its selection framework — the supplied guidance specifies none, while the Milan criteria carry an age limit under 60 and under 50% liver involvement and ESMO quotes age under 60 and Ki-67 under 10%. Whether the programme opens a NELM transplant protocol at all is unresolved decision 5.

avoid.t: Do not take the published series' criteria as evidence-derived thresholds.
avoid.pref: They are protocol conditions: well-differentiated G1–G2 disease, portal-drained primary already resected, liver-only disease, hepatic involvement below a defined threshold, an age limit, and a documented period of stability before listing.
avoid.avoid: Reading them as a selection rule validated against outcome. The Milan-NET criteria were proposed in 2007, before the cohort they are now quoted from, so the 2016 analysis measures the outcome of patients chosen by the criteria rather than testing the criteria themselves. They do not include nodal status of the primary, yet nodal involvement was the only independent predictor of post-transplant survival in the resection comparison (hazard ratio 5.7, 1.3–24) while liver involvement above 50% and G3 tumour were not — the criteria may be selecting on the wrong variable. ESMO's version of the same thresholds carries level IV evidence and is tighter than several published series.
