quickref.title: Cytoreduction thresholds, and what supports them
quickref.intro: Five different debulking targets are in circulation; this is where each comes from.
rows: More than 90% of metastatic disease — NCCN

May provide symptomatic relief, prevent future symptoms and improve progression-free survival. NANETS 2017 records that the historic 90% figure came from an observation on symptom relief and was never validated as an oncologic threshold
At least 70% of visible liver disease — NANETS 2017, small bowel

Near consensus with one dissent: any number or size of metastases, intermediate grade and extrahepatic disease allowed if 70% is achievable. Over 70% versus under 70% gave median overall survival not reached versus 6.5 years (P=0.009) and progression-free survival 3.2 versus 1.3 years (P<0.001) — in two retrospective single-institution series from the centres that championed the lower threshold
More than 70%, individualised — NANETS 2020, pancreas

No consensus reached. Over half the panel favoured it over the traditional 90%; progression-free survival was 10.8, 20.6 and 56.1 months and median overall survival 37.6 months, 134.4 months and not reached for under 70%, 70–90% and over 90%, with the upper two not differing from each other. Some members held that only complete clearance helps and a minority doubted any benefit has been established
70–90% or more — ENETS 2023, functioning pancreatic NET
Level 2b, grade B, with adequate liver function; the paper gives no guidance on which end of the 20-point range applies to whom
An unreviewed note only: surgery and liver-directed therapy were excluded from the systematic review, so a surgical reader should not treat it as that guideline's evidence
No threshold at all — ENETS 2024 small intestine, ESMO 2020

ENETS 2024 does not address the 70 versus 90 question and sets no Ki-67 cutoff for operating on resectable liver metastases; ESMO gives no cytoreduction target, endorses debulking for hormonal symptoms and calls its role in non-functioning disease unclear
quickref.foot: No comparative study supports either number as a threshold. The series most often cited for 70% is one expanded-criteria cohort of 52 patients: retrospective, single-surgeon, single-institution, with the debulking percentage taken as the operating surgeon's own intraoperative visual and ultrasonographic estimate, and that same surgeon deciding who was operated on at all — patients in whom 70% was judged unachievable intraoperatively were not resected, so the cohort has no sub-70% arm and cannot test the threshold. Within it the extent of debulking did not correlate with liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37), progression rates were 27.3%, 27.3% and 31.6% across the three groups (P=.95), and complete resection of all gross disease in 12 of 52 (25%) conferred no advantage; the group sizes were 11 at 70–89%, 22 at 90–99% and 19 at 100%. No morbidity or mortality rate is reported anywhere in the paper — only a median length of stay of 6 days. 88% were kept on octreotide LAR, which the authors say may itself account for the long progression-free survival, and median follow-up was 37.4 months against a median liver progression-free survival of 71.6 months. The NANETS comparisons quoted above are within-cohort retrospective contrasts in which the panel itself notes that patients offered more complete cytoreduction had more favourable disease. The hepatic burden threshold above which cytoreduction is not attempted remains unresolved local decision 3.

quickref.foot: Crisis after 177Lu-dotatate is estimated at 1 to 2% of recipients, but that figure comes from a narrative review — no search dates, strings or quality appraisal — whose authors state the diagnosis lacks agreed criteria and whose own 127 administrations over five years produced none; surgical series cited by NANETS report intraoperative event rates of 24 to 30% despite octreotide, including in patients without the syndrome, with liver metastases the strongest predictor in one of them. So the number given to a PRRT patient and the number given to a surgical patient come from different literatures and disagree by an order of magnitude. Octreotide within 48 hours, or octreotide LAR within 28 days, of 177Lu-dotatate can competitively block tumour uptake and reduce efficacy, and no rule defines when prophylaxis is worth that trade-off.

honest.t: Hepatic cytoreduction should clear at least 70% of visible disease.
honest.why: No comparative study supports 70%, or 90%, as a threshold. The 90% figure NCCN still prints came from an observation about symptom relief and was never validated as an oncologic threshold. The 70% figure was set by the NANETS 2017 panel, with one dissenting vote, on two retrospective single-institution series from the centres that championed it. The series on which it chiefly rests enrolled 52 patients and excluded by design every patient in whom the operating surgeon judged intraoperatively that 70% was unachievable, so it contains no sub-70% group and cannot test the threshold at all; within it the extent of debulking did not correlate with liver progression-free survival (P=.74) or disease-specific survival (P=.37), the three debulking groups progressed at 27.3%, 27.3% and 31.6% (P=.95), and the lowest group holds 11 patients. NANETS 2020 reached no consensus on any threshold for pancreatic primaries, over half the panel favouring an individualised 70% and a minority questioning whether any benefit of cytoreduction has been established. What should drive the decision is whether a named target can be cleared in a patient fit for a long operation with enough functional parenchyma left, not a percentage. The programme tracks burden before and after, the residual left behind, and liver progression-free survival.

honest.t: The debulking series show what an operation delivers.
honest.why: They show what selected patients did. Five-year disease-specific survival of 90% and a median liver progression-free survival of 71.6 months come from a retrospective, single-surgeon, single-institution cohort of 52 patients in which the debulking percentage was the operating surgeon's own visual and ultrasonographic estimate and the same surgeon chose who was operated on. The only variable that predicted outcome was age — 5-year liver progression-free survival 25.7% under 50 versus 85% at 50 or older. 88% of patients were maintained on octreotide LAR, which the authors themselves say may account for the unusually long progression-free survival rather than the debulking strategy, and median follow-up of 37.4 months falls short of the median it reports. No morbidity or mortality rate appears anywhere in the paper, only a median length of stay of 6 days, so a patient cannot be quoted a complication risk from it. Present these figures as the outcomes of selected patients and quote institutional morbidity from the programme's own registry instead.

honest.t: Operating on liver-only stage IV disease when R0 is achievable is a curative-intent option.
honest.why: ENETS 2024 does recommend it, at B-4 — among the weakest grades in that document — on 5-year overall survival of 71 to 74%, and 85% for R0 resections. The same paper records recurrence after R0 of about 80% at 5 years, and ESMO attributes the 85% partly to preselection bias and notes that liver metastases are often more extensive than appreciated even intraoperatively. So R0 here buys a long interval, not a cure, and the consent conversation should say so and commit to lifelong follow-up.

honest.t: A somatostatin analogue controls tumour growth in neuroendocrine liver metastases.
honest.why: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials met their primary endpoints, which is why this remains grade A, but neither population resembles a high-burden liver patient. PROMID's effect was concentrated where there was least liver to treat — hazard ratio 0.17 (0.08–0.40) at 0 to 10% hepatic involvement, 0.40 (0.10–1.67) at 10 to 50% and 0.71 (0.11–4.45) above 50% — with 95% of patients at Ki-67 of 2% or less, and it is an interim analysis of a trial closed at 85 of a planned 162 patients whose confirmatory survival analysis was never done. CLARINET did hold above 25% hepatic volume, hazard ratio 0.45 (0.22–0.91), but that dichotomy is a post hoc simplification of a prespecified five-category variable and 96% of its patients were not progressing at entry. Neither showed an overall-survival or quality-of-life benefit, and the effect is stabilisation, not shrinkage: one partial remission per arm in PROMID. An analogue is not a substitute for a liver plan in a patient whose liver is the problem.

honest.t: Continuing an analogue after progression is wrong, or right.
honest.why: Neither has been shown. No trial tested continuation after documented progression in either direction: PROMID and CLARINET both enrolled patients who were not progressing, and the NANETS midgut panel reached no consensus on the question. The roadmap's position — that the indication after progression is hormonal rather than antiproliferative — is a defensible reading of what the trials enrolled, not a demonstrated equivalence, and the string is graded C for that reason. What should drive the decision is whether the analogue is doing hormonal work nothing else in the plan replaces.

honest.t: PRRT prolongs survival in neuroendocrine tumours.
honest.why: It has never been shown to. NETTER-1's prespecified final overall-survival analysis did not meet its endpoint: 48.0 versus 36.3 months, hazard ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.17), p=0.30. It was a secondary endpoint powered for 158 deaths and the 5-year calendar cutoff arrived first at 142; the proportional-hazards assumption failed, so the hazard ratio is not a valid single summary; 36% of controls crossed over, making the comparison closer to early versus delayed PRRT than to PRRT versus none; and the restricted-mean-survival analysis that carries the authors' positive message was added by protocol amendment and does not exclude zero at 5 years. NETTER-2's overall survival is immature with 48% crossover and showed no difference in time to deterioration of global health status, diarrhoea, fatigue or pain. What PRRT has shown is a large and reproducible progression-free survival and response effect. Say that, and nothing more, to a patient.

honest.t: The first-line PRRT evidence applies to the patients on this page.
honest.why: Only partly. NETTER-2 enrolled newly diagnosed disease within 6 months of diagnosis, with no patient having progressed on a prior analogue, uptake score 3 or 4 required in every target lesion, and — decisively for a liver pathway — any previous hepatic artery embolisation or radiofrequency ablation as an exclusion. That removes heterogeneous-uptake disease and most of the population gate 7 of this page creates. 54% of its patients had pancreatic primaries, so it is not a midgut trial, and its comparator was high-dose octreotide 60 mg, which the authors themselves describe as giving 4 to 8 months of progression-free survival in grade 3 disease. There is no comparison with the alkylating chemotherapy a board would weigh first line in a high-grade pancreatic NET. EANM Focus 3 supported first-line PRRT only in a minority of highly selected patients (17 of 22, 77.3%). Whether the programme offers first-line PRRT, and to whom, stays an approval item.

honest.t: The PRRT label describes the evidence.
honest.why: The approval covers SSTR-positive GEP-NET including foregut, midgut and hindgut tumours; NETTER-1 enrolled only jejunoileal and proximal colon primaries with Ki-67 of 20% or less and OctreoScan-defined uptake. Everything outside midgut rests on retrospective and registry series — which is why EANM declined to recommend PRRT second line for pancreatic NET at all, why ESMO places it in pancreatic NET only after failure of approved therapies [III, A], and why NANETS/SNMMI scores pancreatic use 8 rather than 9. Eligibility today is set by 68Ga- or 64Cu-DOTATATE PET, not by the scintigraphy the trial used, so even the midgut population is not quite the one being selected.

honest.t: There is a right sequence for systemic therapy after progression.
honest.why: ASCO states explicitly that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any particular sequence, because the trials used placebo controls with almost no head-to-head comparisons; its own recommendations in this space are graded weak on low to moderate evidence quality, and it rated overall-survival certainty very low for CLARINET, RADIANT-3, RADIANT-4 and the sunitinib trial and low for NETTER-1. Itanet's preferences for radioligand therapy over targeted agents (2b-B) and over chemotherapy (3b-A) are explicitly built on cross-trial comparison and retrospective series, and ESMO records that one of its own authors dissented on PRRT sequencing. The order chosen for a patient should be recorded at board with its reason — primary site, receptor status, growth rate, hepatic burden, need for rapid shrinkage, prior therapy, toxicity tolerance and access — and tracked in the registry, because the registry is the only place a local sequence will ever be evaluated.

honest.t: Capecitabine–temozolomide is the agent to choose when shrinkage is wanted quickly.
honest.why: Its response rate did not differ from single-agent temozolomide — 39.7% versus 33.8%, P=0.59 — in a trial not powered for response, so the rationale for choosing it on shrinkage is weak. E2211 is a phase 2 trial declared positive at an interim analysis with an adjusted two-sided alpha of 0.119, designed at a two-sided significance level of 0.20; the effect weakened from hazard ratio 0.58 (0.36–0.93) at interim to 0.71 (0.46–1.07) at final analysis, overall survival was not significant (53.8 versus 58.7 months, hazard ratio 0.82, P=.42) after a significant interim difference failed to persist, grade 3–4 toxicity doubled to 45%, and the control arm was never a standard of care. It remains a reasonable choice for high-burden or rapidly progressing pancreatic disease, but on burden and tempo rather than on an expectation of response.

honest.t: The targeted agents delay progression, so they are doing something to the tumour.
honest.why: They stabilise it. Confirmed objective response was 5% in RADIANT-3, 2% in RADIANT-4, 9.3% with sunitinib and 5 to 19% with cabozantinib, so none of them will convert unresectable hepatic disease. None has an established survival benefit: RADIANT-3's overall survival is uninterpretable after 73% crossover, RADIANT-4's was a first interim look at 70 deaths of a planned 191 that missed its boundary by orders of magnitude, the sunitinib trial closed early at 171 of 340 patients without crossing its efficacy boundary (z 3.85 against 3.88) with censoring of 65% versus 40%, and CABINET showed no survival difference in either cohort and stopped early on local rather than central assessment. In RADIANT-4 the size of the effect depended on who read the scans — 11.0 versus 3.9 months centrally against 14.0 versus 5.5 locally.

honest.t: The systemic trials tell us how to combine drugs with liver-directed therapy.
honest.why: None of them can. RADIANT-3 and RADIANT-4 excluded patients embolised within 6 months or ablated within 2 months; NETTER-2 excluded any prior hepatic artery embolisation or ablation outright; RETNET excluded prior hepatic arterial or hepatic radiation therapy and allowed no concomitant therapy beyond octreotide or bisphosphonates. The trial populations were built by removing exactly the patients this page's liver-directed gates produce. NANETS states plainly that cumulative hepatic radiation from radioembolisation followed by PRRT is unstudied, and NANETS/SNMMI that prior liver-directed therapy raises concern for PRRT hepatotoxicity. Cumulative hepatic-directed exposure per patient is therefore a registry field, not a calculation anyone can do from the literature.

honest.t: Debulking before PRRT improves the response.
honest.why: NANETS/SNMMI says it may, and attributes that to limited retrospective data — a single series. The parallel argument, that debulking before a radioligand course reduces the mass of amine-producing cells and so the crisis risk, comes from a narrative review. Both are reasons to proceed when cytoreduction is independently justified in a fit patient with high hepatic burden; neither is a reason to operate on someone who would not otherwise be a cytoreduction candidate. It is the one place where the surgeon sits inside the PRRT safety pathway rather than beside it, which is also why the indication is easy to inflate.

honest.t: Bland embolisation and conventional chemoembolisation are interchangeable.
honest.why: They may not be, and the guidelines disagree. The largest technique comparison is a retrospective, non-randomised MD Anderson cohort in which treatment was chosen by the referring physician: in 69 carcinoid patients bland embolisation gave a response of 81.0% against 44.4% for chemoembolisation (odds ratio 6.41, 1.97–20.84, P=0.002) with no difference in progression-free or overall survival, while in 54 islet-cell patients chemoembolisation trended better but those patients had more resected primaries and less liver involvement. ENETS 2024 generally prefers bland embolisation in small-intestine NET; ENETS 2023 calls chemoembolisation possibly more effective in functioning pancreatic NET. The only randomised comparison in the literature is 26 patients and underpowered, and the three-way prospective trial that would answer it is still running. The default is an expertise and availability decision, and it belongs to the programme, with technique, stated goal, hepatic progression-free survival and toxicity recorded for every procedure.

honest.t: RETNET established something about embolisation technique.
honest.why: The RETNET paper in this depot is the published study protocol and reports no outcome data of any kind — no response, no progression-free survival, no survival. Its quantitative content is a power calculation resting on retrospective single-centre estimates of 11 months of hepatic progression-free survival for bland embolisation against 20 for lipiodol chemoembolisation, with the assumption that lipiodol and drug-eluting chemoembolisation are equivalent on safety, which the trial itself then disproved. Its practice-changing message came from the 20% serious-adverse-event stopping rule that closed the drug-eluting-bead arm, a closure reported in the ENETS 2024 guidance rather than in the protocol paper. Any outcome figure attributed to RETNET anywhere in the programme's material — including the shared liver-directed-therapy matrix, which carries such figures for this disease — is unsourced and should be removed at source.

honest.t: Drug-eluting embolics are unsafe in neuroendocrine tumours.
honest.why: The position is kept, and the string is downgraded to C to say what it rests on. The phase 2 trial is a single-centre interrupted interim analysis of 13 patients, so neither the 54% biloma rate nor the response rate has a usable confidence interval. The injury fell on patients with roughly one third the hepatic tumour burden of those spared (mean 12% versus 44%, P=0.06), the beads were mixed 1:1 with contrast and invisible on injection with the endpoint judged by operator tactile feedback, and the authors concede this may have caused overembolisation and non-target deposition. The 54% figure is far out of line with the comparator series the paper itself cites — about 30% biliary injury needing no drainage in one, 0% in another using 500 to 700 micrometre particles. The confirmatory signal is an arm closure in an ongoing trial, reported in a guideline. Two patients died and the injury is biliary and irreversible, which is reason enough for a precautionary institutional ban; it is not a demonstrated class effect.

honest.t: Radioembolisation gives a 70-month median survival in this disease.
honest.why: That number comes from a voluntary 10-centre retrospective series of 148 patients in which 78% were still alive at a median follow-up of 42 months, so the estimate is immature and heavily censored; response assessment was not standardised, using CT, MRI or scintigraphy with each investigator giving a best estimate where WHO or RECIST could not be applied; half the patients came from self-described centres of excellence; and neither grade nor Ki-67 is reported. The single-centre series that followed the same technique for long-term toxicity reported a median survival of 28.0 months in 93 patients, and showed that two baseline findings dominate the conversation — 7.3 months with ascites against 53.8 without, 21.1 months with extrahepatic disease against 58.0 without. Quote those, and the patient's own baseline, rather than the 70-month figure.

honest.t: Late hepatic injury after radioembolisation is quantified.
honest.why: It is signalled, not quantified. Cirrhosis-like morphology or portal-hypertension signs appeared in 15 of 52 patients (29%) followed beyond a year, more often after bilobar treatment, but no single imaging finding reached significance and the series was not powered for it; the sustained ALP and AST elevation beyond four years is a finding in 11 people. The denominator shrinks as it goes: of 93 patients treated, 41 had under a year of follow-up, 23 were lost and 18 died. Nine of the 52 had systemic therapy in the first year, 24 had prior chemoembolisation or bland embolisation and 21 prior resection, and the authors state these and tumour progression could not be separated from the radiation. No radioembolisation-induced liver failure occurred in that series or in the 148-patient series. The honest position is that the risk is real, undefined in size, and concentrated in bilobar treatment — which is why a long expected survival raises the threshold rather than lowering it, and why long-term hepatic follow-up for every treated patient is a dashboard item.

honest.t: Adding radioembolisation to PRRT improves hepatic control.
honest.why: On one comparison of a prospective single-arm cohort against a retrospective historical control, with 24 of a planned 120 pairs matched. Two-year hepatic progression-free survival was 82% versus 50% and best objective response 71% versus 25%, but median progression-free and overall survival were unseparated, there was no survival benefit, the proportion of deaths was higher in the combination arm, and the toxicity and hormonal-symptom analyses were abandoned because the retrospective arm's reporting was unreliable. Median liver tumour burden in the matched set was 8% versus 20%, so this is not a bulky-disease population; ECOG could not be balanced and every combination patient dropped at least one point after PRRT before the SIRT; and the study was funded by the microsphere manufacturer with two of its employees as co-authors. There is still no evidence either way on the safety of sequencing radioembolisation and PRRT.

honest.t: Thermal ablation can be complete local treatment for four lesions or fewer each under 3 cm.
honest.why: That limit is not where the evidence comes from. NCCN states it and ENETS 2024 puts percutaneous ablation at three to five metastases each under 3 cm at B-3, but the two series behind ablation in this disease enrolled up to 15 tumours, up to 10 cm, with under 20% liver volume involved, a mean largest tumour of 3.6 cm and a mean of six lesions treated. Quote local control per patient as well as per lesion — recurrence at an ablated site in 11% and 22% of patients against 6.3% and 7.9% of lesions — and note that 80% of one series developed new or progressive liver disease and 63% and 59% of the larger series developed new liver and new extrahepatic disease. Neither series reports grade or Ki-67; at the published discussion the authors confirmed the analysis was never done. Both pool medullary thyroid carcinoma and bronchial carcinoids with gastroenteropancreatic disease, and outcomes are confounded by salvage in 30% on an analogue, 27% re-ablated, 18% on chemotherapy and 10% embolised. There is no established cured fraction; record residual disease and grade instead.

honest.t: Resecting the primary in the presence of unresectable liver metastases prolongs survival.
honest.why: NANETS reached full consensus that it should be considered in small-bowel primaries, on retrospective medians of 7.4 versus 4.0 years, 9.9 versus 4.7 years and 159 versus 47 months — all from cohorts in which the unresected patients were older, more comorbid or more heavily liver-replaced, which NANETS states cannot be separated from the effect. ENETS adds that at least three propensity-matched studies show no survival benefit in asymptomatic stage IV disease, and that only 22% of a watch-and-wait cohort ever needed surgery. NANETS 2020 reached no consensus for pancreatic primaries, the majority holding that resection may help only in selected circumstances. The defensible reasons to operate are the complications for which no effective therapy exists — obstruction, mesenteric ischaemia, bleeding, perforation — and transplant candidacy; survival is not one of them.

honest.t: Transplantation for neuroendocrine liver metastases gives 10-year survival near 90%.
honest.why: That figure rests on 42 transplanted patients at one centre over 15 years. 280 referrals produced 88 patients meeting Milan-NET criteria, 42 of whom were transplanted and 46 not, the split driven by waiting-list capacity, age and patient refusal. Recipients were 15 years younger in a cohort where age independently predicted death; 18 of the 22 who declined did so because they judged their own health normal, so the comparison arm is self-selected on wellbeing; the non-transplant arm predates current therapy, with 8.7% having PRRT and none a cytoreductive liver resection; and WHO 2010 review reclassified 8.7% of them as G3 against none of the recipients. The cohort was too small to match on, so propensity score entered only as a covariate, giving an adjusted benefit of 6.82 months at 5 years (95% CI 1.10–12.54) rising to 38.43 months at 10 years. 88% of grafts were marginal quality, and 6 of the 9 deaths after transplantation were from transplant sequelae rather than cancer. The companion resection comparison is univariate only, over 36 years, with transplant recipients selected by a test of time — median 38.5 months from primary resection to liver surgery against 6.5 — and a resection arm that had no routine lymphadenectomy and 11% R1 margins. Enough to justify a protocol and a registry; not enough to make transplantation a routine option.

honest.t: The Milan-NET criteria are validated selection thresholds.
honest.why: They are protocol conditions published in 2007, before the cohort now quoted from them, so the 2016 analysis measures the outcome of patients chosen by the criteria rather than testing the criteria. They omit nodal status of the primary, yet nodal involvement was the only independent predictor of post-transplant survival in the resection comparison (hazard ratio 5.7, 1.3–24) while liver involvement above 50% and G3 histology were not — the criteria may be selecting on the wrong variable. The thresholds also disagree across sources: Milan sets age under 60 as a relative criterion and under 50% liver volume, ESMO quotes age under 60 with Ki-67 under 10% at level IV, and the OPTN review-board guidance states no age limit and no hepatic burden cutoff at all. Any local age or burden limit must therefore be labelled local or attributed to its selection framework.

honest.t: The transplant decision is settled by the transplant criteria.
honest.why: Two other things settle it first. Limited disease amenable to curative liver resection excluded 75 of 280 referrals in the Milan series, so the commonest reason not to transplant a Milan-in patient is that an operation would clear the liver; favourable-biology patients are usually cytoreduction candidates too, and resection and cytoreduction must be compared against transplantation at the same board before listing. And allocation is separate from benefit: neuroendocrine liver metastasis is not a standardised OPTN MELD exception, so listing goes by the nonstandard 'other liver cancer or tumour, specify' route with a written narrative at MMaT-3, with 90-day extensions, and NCCN still deems transplantation investigational. ENETS 2024 reduces transplantation to a rare consideration in selected individuals. Whether the programme opens a NELM transplant protocol at all remains an approval item.

honest.t: Imaging-timing wording for the transplant exception means what it sounds like.
honest.why: It does not, and the page deliberately reproduces it unchanged. The review-board guidance requires radiologic workup for extrahepatic disease 'at least 3 months prior to initial or extension MELD exception request (submit date)', including somatostatin-receptor scintigraphy or Ga-68 imaging or PET. Read literally that is a floor on how old the imaging must be, which is the opposite of what a clinician assumes; the intended timing is confirmed with the review process before filing while current clinical staging is kept. MMaT also means the median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run, not a fixed national score, and an MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15 under Policy 9.4.E. These are policy mechanics, not evidence, and they are the commonest source of a failed listing.

honest.t: Prophylactic octreotide prevents intraoperative carcinoid crisis.
honest.why: NCCN states it is likely ineffective, NANETS 2017 says prevention has not been established, and NANETS 2020 calls the role of analogues in preventing crisis in pancreatic NET undefined. The NANETS 2017 recommendation is internally conflicted, stating that the literature does not support prophylaxis while sanctioning an intraoperative infusion of 100 to 500 micrograms per hour as harmless practice. The incidence figures themselves disagree by an order of magnitude depending on which literature is read: 1 to 2% during 177Lu-dotatate from a narrative review whose authors say the diagnosis lacks agreed criteria and whose own 127 administrations produced no crisis, against intraoperative event rates of 24 to 30% despite octreotide in surgical series, with liver metastases the strongest predictor in one. What should drive practice is preparedness — a named owner per procedure, rescue octreotide in the room, and fluids and vasopressors that octreotide must never delay — audited for adherence rather than for effectiveness.

honest.t: Pre-procedure octreotide is simply good practice before a hepatic procedure.
honest.why: It carries a cost that no rule prices. Octreotide within 48 hours, or octreotide LAR within 28 days, of 177Lu-dotatate can competitively block tumour uptake and reduce efficacy, and the review that records this offers no rule for when prophylaxis is worth the trade-off beyond individual judgement. So in a functional patient heading for a radioligand course the prophylaxis decision has to be made explicitly with nuclear medicine rather than by default, and documented either way.

honest.t: Functional status and hepatic burden and distribution are named requirements at grade D.
honest.why: The roadmap grades them D because no comparative study tests the thresholds themselves. They are kept because functional status changes procedural safety planning and not only symptom management, and because a pathway cannot be assigned without knowing which problem is driving the clinical picture. Audit them for completeness at submission, not for effect.

honest.t: Differentiation and grade reporting is a grade B requirement.
honest.why: It is now graded C. The requirement is right and the pathway cannot run without it, but its evidence is consensus, not comparison: NANETS 2017 means a show of hands from a 15-member panel with no evidence grading and no systematic search, which recorded consensus that both differentiation and grade be reported and a significant majority that both mitotic rate and Ki-67 be measured. The Ki-67 55% discriminator between carcinoma and well-differentiated G3 comes from a single report, and the same ENETS paper concedes morphology can be ambiguous, particularly for large-cell carcinoma. ENETS 2023 also excludes well-differentiated G3 from its scope by design, so the guidance is strongest exactly where the diagnosis is already unambiguous and silent where the fork actually bites.

honest.t: Imaging every 3 to 4 months at first, then about every 6 months once stable.
honest.why: A local interval chosen within the NCCN range of every 12 weeks to 12 months, retained where risk warrants it rather than claiming one NCCN interval for every patient. ASCO suggests every 3 to 6 months in low-volume asymptomatic disease and NANETS suggests 3 to 4 months if observing; no trial compares surveillance intervals, and the three published ranges are not the same. Observation itself is an equally acceptable course in this phenotype rather than an inferior one: the NANETS panel split roughly evenly, and the CLARINET placebo arm ran a median 18.0 months without progression.

honest.t: A mandatory exhaustion-of-all-options rule before radioembolisation is a local restriction, not NCCN.
honest.why: The roadmap says so explicitly and now permits phenotype-selected Y90 as a reasonable consideration. The counterweight is not evidence of harm from early use but the treatment-horizon principle: a long expected survival raises the threshold for hepatic radioembolisation rather than lowering it, because radiation-induced liver injury accrues over exactly the time the patient has, and the size of that risk is undefined. NANETS itself reached no consensus on a preferred embolisation modality and judged the evidence insufficient for second-line use while supporting it later for liver-dominant disease.

honest.t: The tumour board operating model is labelled Standard because the programme has chosen it, not because trials support it.
honest.why: The roadmap says these are stakeholder-derived operating requirements, reproduced unchanged across every disease roadmap so the programme has one operating standard rather than five, evidence grade D by construction. Audit them for adherence, not for effectiveness.

honest.t: Poorly differentiated carcinoma is excluded from liver-directed and transplant pathways on strong evidence.
honest.why: The exclusion is right and the grading is honest about why it is not strong. ENETS grades both the advice against metastasectomy and the advice against PRRT in metastatic digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma 5D, its weakest grade, resting on no comparative data; almost every therapeutic recommendation in that paper is 4B or weaker and no randomised trial underpins either first- or second-line therapy. What carries the decision is the natural history rather than a trial: SEER median survival of 5.2 months for distant disease with 4.7% alive at 5 years, 11 to 12 months on palliative platinum–etoposide against about 1 month without it, and performance status dominating everything (18, 12 and 5 months at PS 0, 1 and 2). In a disease measured in months, a liver-directed plan without an end date is the harm.

honest.t: Well-differentiated G3 disease has a defined surgical position.
honest.why: It does not, and this is the gap a liver surgeon will meet first. The roadmap does not say whether hepatic debulking is appropriate in well-differentiated G3 disease. NANETS 2017 refers grade 3 liver metastases for systemic therapy; NANETS 2020 says poorly differentiated carcinoma should not be resected while localised well-differentiated G3 tumours may be resected within multimodal therapy with liver cytoreduction often not indicated — and states in the same paper that its well-differentiated G3 recommendations are unsupported, pending studies using the 2017 WHO classification. ENETS 2023 excludes well-differentiated G3 from its scope; ASCO allows the whole G1–G2 menu on informal consensus rated very low quality and supports no Ki-67 cutoff. Meanwhile NETTER-2 gives this phenotype the strongest randomised systemic evidence on the page. Eligibility for a G3 systemic option is not eligibility for cytoreduction or transplantation, and alignment area 15 asks for the G3 debulking position to be settled explicitly.

board: Submission: an Epic form capturing the clinical question, differentiation and Ki-67, somatostatin-receptor status, functional syndrome status, hepatic burden and distribution, primary site and whether resected, extrahepatic sites, prior therapy, referring clinician and urgency. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage: the coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check completeness, imaging quality, duplicate cases, the urgent lane, and whether the question is a decision question. Owner: coordinator and chair.
Agenda: stable at least 24 hours ahead, approximately 10 to 12 decision cases per session, each carrying one focused question. Owner: coordinator.
Urgent lane: a same-week slot with chair approval, used in this disease for uncontrolled hormonal syndromes and for suspected high-grade transformation. Owner: chair.

Attendance: hepatobiliary and transplant surgery, medical oncology, nuclear medicine or theranostics, interventional radiology, diagnostic radiology, pathology, endocrinology where functional disease is managed, and coordination. Owner: specialty leads.

Imaging: adequate and available current imaging reviewed before the recommendation, with the somatostatin-receptor PET/CT result available or its absence explicitly noted. Owner: diagnostic radiology and nuclear medicine.
Pathology: pre-alerted for every case requiring differentiation, grade, Ki-67, or re-biopsy for suspected transformation. Owner: pathology.

Output: one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, one documented alternative considered — and where the tumour is functional, the carcinoid-crisis prophylaxis owner named separately. Owner: chair.
Documentation: an Epic note within one business day in the agreed structured format. Owner: named owner.
Registry: the case closed with the decision, the modality delivered, cumulative hepatic-directed exposure, and the outcome at reassessment. Owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships: the referring clinician is informed of the recommendation and who owns the next step; community-referring relationships are protected explicitly — the pathway returns patients with a plan, it does not capture them. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Embolisation: technique, stated goal, hepatic progression-free survival and toxicity, recorded for every procedure.
PRRT: every course, with progression-free survival and hepatic and renal function.
Cytoreduction: hepatic burden before and after, the residual left behind, and liver progression-free survival.
Radioembolisation: long-term hepatic follow-up for every patient treated, with cumulative hepatic-directed exposure per patient.
Transplantation: registry entry for every listing, with the allocation record and a named renewal owner.
Functional disease: carcinoid-crisis prophylaxis documented before every procedure, audited for adherence.
Re-biopsy: rate, and whether the pathway changed when it was performed.
Board output: named owner, due date and reassessment date present on every recommendation, with the Epic note filed within one business day.
Every repeat liver-directed cycle: the viable target, the goal (symptoms or progression), the liver-function cost, the owner and the reassessment date all named.
Source currency: NCCN edition and OPTN allocation requirements verified on the agreed cycle by a named owner.

approvals.q: Which embolisation technique is the programme's default?
approvals.why: The only prospective three-way comparison is still enrolling and its drug-eluting-bead arm closed for severe complications. One small randomised TAE versus TACE trial (Maire 2012, 26 patients, cited from ENETS rather than read in full) found no significant 2-year progression-free survival difference but was underpowered. The best non-randomised comparison favours bland embolisation on response in carcinoid disease (81.0% versus 44.4%, odds ratio 6.41) with no survival difference, but treatment was chosen by the referring physician; ENETS 2024 prefers bland in small-intestine NET while ENETS 2023 calls chemoembolisation possibly more effective in functioning pancreatic NET. Any choice is expertise and availability.
approvals.audit: Registry: technique, goal, hepatic progression-free survival, toxicity.

approvals.q: Is first-line PRRT offered for receptor-positive grade 2–3 disease, and to whom?
approvals.why: One open-label randomised trial with a progression-free survival endpoint; overall survival immature. Depends on radiopharmaceutical availability and payer authorisation.
approvals.audit: Registry: every PRRT course, progression-free survival, hepatic and renal function.

approvals.q: Hepatic burden threshold above which cytoreduction is not attempted.
approvals.why: Debulking series are single-arm and selection-driven and no threshold is evidence-derived. The 90% figure was an observation about symptom relief, never validated oncologically; the 70% figure was set by consensus on two retrospective series from the championing centres, and the cohort most cited for it excluded by design every patient in whom 70% was unachievable, so it has no sub-70% arm. NANETS 2020 reached no consensus for pancreatic primaries.
approvals.audit: Registry: burden before and after, residual, liver progression-free survival.

approvals.q: Does the programme offer radioembolisation in this disease at all, and at what point?
approvals.why: Evidence is minimal and the long treatment horizon makes cumulative hepatic radiation injury the dominant consideration.
approvals.audit: Registry required if offered; long-term hepatic follow-up.

approvals.q: Does the programme open a NELM transplant protocol?
approvals.why: Non-randomised series: 42 transplanted patients at one centre over 15 years, with recipients 15 years younger, a self-selected comparison arm, a pre-targeted-therapy comparator and 88% marginal grafts; adjustment for measured factors narrowed the benefit to 6.82 months at 5 years and unmeasured selection remains, and 6 of the 9 deaths after transplantation were from transplant sequelae. NCCN still calls transplantation investigational and NELM is a nonstandard exception, not a standardised one. Graft stewardship is an institutional judgement.

approvals.q: Who owns carcinoid-crisis prophylaxis, and how is it verified before each procedure?
approvals.why: Not an evidence question. It is a named safety process that fails when it lives in individual memory.
approvals.audit: Audit: prophylaxis documented before every procedure in functional patients.

approvals.q: Re-biopsy policy for suspected grade progression or transformation.
approvals.why: No evidence defines the trigger or interval; behaviour-driven in practice.
approvals.audit: Audit: re-biopsy rate, change in pathway when performed.

approvals.q: Who owns subsequent NCCN and OPTN update checks, and on what cycle?
approvals.why: Source reconciliation is complete in this version. An owner is assigned to verify subsequent editions and current allocation requirements, ratify the documented institutional positions, and maintain the update cycle.
approvals.audit: Named owner plus edition and date plus update cycle.

approvals.q: Is hepatic debulking offered in well-differentiated G3 disease, and under what conditions?
approvals.why: The roadmap is silent and the guidelines conflict. Both NANETS surgical papers advise against cytoreducing G3 liver metastases, NANETS 2020 conceding that its well-differentiated G3 recommendations are unsupported; ENETS 2023 excludes well-differentiated G3 by scope; ASCO permits the G1–G2 menu on very low quality informal consensus. NETTER-2 meanwhile gives this phenotype the strongest randomised systemic evidence on the page, so the surgical question will be asked at board. Alignment area 15.
approvals.audit: Registry: every G3 hepatic operation with differentiation, Ki-67, residual disease and liver progression-free survival.

approvals.q: Is first-line PRRT offered to a patient who has already had liver-directed therapy?
approvals.why: NETTER-2 excluded any previous hepatic artery embolisation or radiofrequency ablation, and required uptake score 3 or 4 in every target lesion, so the first-line evidence does not describe this patient at all. NANETS states cumulative hepatic radiation from radioembolisation followed by PRRT is unstudied, and NANETS/SNMMI that prior liver-directed therapy raises concern for PRRT hepatotoxicity.
approvals.audit: Registry: cumulative hepatic-directed exposure before each PRRT course, with hepatic and renal function.

approvals.q: Does the programme reproduce or restate the NCCN position against drug-eluting embolics, and on what basis?
approvals.why: The position is kept but it is a precautionary institutional choice, not a demonstrated class effect: a 13-patient interrupted interim analysis in which bilomas fell on the lowest-burden patients, with invisible beads and a tactile endpoint, and a biliary injury rate far out of line with other drug-eluting series. The confirmatory signal is an arm closure in an ongoing trial reported in a guideline. Stating the basis matters because the harm is irreversible and two patients died.
approvals.audit: Audit: any drug-eluting embolic use in NET recorded as an exception with named approval.

approvals.q: Who corrects the shared liver-directed-therapy matrix entry that attributes outcome figures to RETNET?
approvals.why: The RETNET paper is a published protocol with no outcome data of any kind, so any response, progression-free survival or survival figure attributed to it is unsourced. The matrix is shared across pathways, so the correction has to be made at its source and the other pathways checked for the same entry.
approvals.audit: Source-currency check: matrix entries reconciled against the depot abstracts by a named owner each cycle.

approvals.q: Which surveillance interval does the programme adopt for observed low-burden disease, and is observation documented as an equal alternative to an immediate analogue?
approvals.why: No trial compares intervals. NCCN allows every 12 weeks to 12 months, ASCO suggests 3 to 6 months, NANETS suggests 3 to 4 months while splitting evenly on whether to observe at all, ENETS restricts watch and wait to selected G1 and ESMO to Ki-67 under 2%. The roadmap's 3-to-4-month choice is local, and alignment area 3 asks whether observation is a documented alternative and whether grade B fits it.
approvals.audit: Audit: documented interval and the alternative considered on every observed patient; progression at first scan after a missed interval.

approvals.q: Who confirms the OPTN imaging-timing wording with the review board before the first NELM filing?
approvals.why: The guidance requires extrahepatic workup 'at least 3 months prior to initial or extension request (submit date)', which read literally is a floor on the age of the imaging rather than the currency requirement a clinician assumes. The page reproduces the wording unchanged rather than correcting it; somebody has to resolve the intent before a listing depends on it.
approvals.audit: Allocation record: imaging dates against submit dates for every request and extension, with the named coordinator's sign-off.
